Never return err (the whole object) and err.stack to clients — even in dev, return message + code only and log the stack server-side. Delete the unused duplicate (errorMiddleware.js) to remove ambiguity, or have one re-export the other.

verdict.note:
Confirmed in code. The claim's mechanics are accurate but its severity narrative is partly off, so I correct it down to medium.

VERIFIED FACTS:
- errorHandler.js:108 gates dev output on `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'`; the production-sanitized branch is the `else` (line 110), so ONLY the literal string 'development' triggers verbose output.
- sendErrorDev (lines 43-61) does return `error: err` (full object) and `stack: err.stack` to the client.
- errorMiddleware.js:38 also gates on 'development' with the same dev-leak pattern (lines 44-45 leak stack).
- Both modules are near-identical duplicates exporting the same names.

CORRECTIONS to the claim:
1. The claim's headline ("leaks whenever NODE_ENV is not exactly 'production'") is BACKWARDS. The verbose dev branch fires ONLY when NODE_ENV === 'development'. For any other non-'production' value (unset, 'prod', 'staging', 'test'), the code falls into the `else`/sanitized branch — which does NOT leak stack/full-error to the client. So the real leak window is the OPPOSITE: a deployment must be explicitly set to 'development' (or left in a dev config) to leak. The description text contradicts itself: it correctly says "Any other value ... falls into the production-sanitized branch in errorHandler.js" but then wrongly concludes leaks occur "without NODE_ENV=production".
2. The wired-in module (server.js:243 imports from errorHandler.js, not errorMiddleware.js) is the safer-defaulting one for the common misconfig of an unset NODE_ENV — unset → else branch → sanitized. errorMiddleware.js is dead code (no importers found via grep).

SEVERITY: The genuine risk is real but conditional: stack-trace/internal-object leakage occurs only when a server is actually run with NODE_ENV=development. Given .env.backup and README default to development, a staging box copying that config WOULD leak — a plausible misconfig. But it requires the explicit 'development' value, not merely "not production" as claimed. That, plus the duplicate-module confusion, makes this a real medium issue rather than high.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: handleDuplicateFieldsDB regex match can throw and crash the error handler itself
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: const value = err.errmsg ? err.errmsg.match(/.../)[0] : 'value'; — String.match returns null when there is no match. On a duplicate-key error whose errmsg does not contain a quoted value (format varies by MongoDB version/driver), [0] is read off null and throws 'Cannot read properties of null'. This throw happens inside the global error handler with no surrounding try/catch, so Express cannot recover and the response hangs / connection is reset. A predictable user action (duplicate registration) can wedge requests.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: const match = err.errmsg && err.errmsg.match(/(["'])(\\?.)*?\1/); const value = match ? match[0] : 'value'; Also prefer err.keyValue (driver provides the offending field/value structured) over regex parsing.

verdict.note: Confirmed at back-end/middleware/errorHandler.js:17: `err.errmsg.match(/(["'])(\\?.)*?\1/)[0]` indexes [0] off a match result with no null check. If errmsg lacks a quoted substring, match() returns null and [0] throws TypeError, inside handleDuplicateFieldsDB called unguarded from the global errorHandler (line 118). A throw inside error-handling middleware is not recovered by Express, so the response hangs. Real latent crash path. Severity lowered to medium: (1) only reachable when NODE_ENV !== 'development' (dev path uses sendErrorDev and skips the duplicate handler); (2) modern MongoDB 11000 errmsg usually DOES contain a quoted value (dup key: { field: \"value\" }), so the no-match case is plausible but not guaranteed on every duplicate — depends on driver version and the duplicated value's type. The 'every duplicate registration wedges requests' framing overstates likelihood.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: PPI weekly cron loads ALL students and processes them serially in one tick — unbounded memory/time and partial-failure crash
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: recalculateAllPpi does Student.find({}) loading every student id into memory, then awaits computeCommunityEngagementScore + findOneAndUpdate serially per student. At scale this is a long-running single-threaded loop that blocks for a long time, holds the connection pool, and a single thrown error aborts the entire batch (no per-student try/catch), so one bad student leaves the rest unprocessed. The alert email then embeds err.stack into HTML (line 53) — internal stack traces emailed in plaintext.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Use a cursor (Student.find().cursor()) or paginate in batches; wrap each student's computation in try/catch and accumulate failures so one failure does not abort the run; process with bounded concurrency (e.g. p-limit). Remove err.stack from the email body or send it only to an internal logging channel, not formatted HTML.

verdict.note: All claimed facts verified in back-end/utils/cronJobs.js. Line 9: Student.find({}).select('_id') loads all students. Lines 10-17: serial per-student loop awaiting computeCommunityEngagementScore + findOneAndUpdate with NO per-student try/catch. The only error handling is the batch-level try/catch in the cron wrapper (lines 39-59), so a single thrown error aborts the whole run, leaving remaining students unprocessed. Line 53 embeds err.stack directly into the alert email HTML. Severity adjusted from high to medium: this is a weekly off-peak cron (Sunday 00:00), not a request path, so the unbounded loop is a bounded operational/scalability concern; the partial-failure-aborts-batch is a genuine correctness bug; and the stack trace is emailed only to the admin/SMTP_USER address, not an external recipient, making the info-disclosure angle minor.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: CourseEnrollment pre-save calls next() twice on happy path and never on course-not-found path
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: In the pre('save') hook, when a course is found with modules, next() is called at line 266 inside the if-block AND again at line 276 at the end of the try. Calling next() twice can trigger 'next() called multiple times' errors and double-execution of downstream middleware. Worse, when the course is NOT found / has no modules (the else branch at line 267-270), only console.warn runs and next() is NEVER called inside that else, so the second next() at 276 saves it — but the structure is fragile and the intended guard (skip flawed progress) is bypassed because execution still falls through to line 276. The duplicate next() is the concrete defect.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Restructure so next() is called exactly once. Remove the next() at line 266. Ensure the inner else (course not found) does NOT fall through to a second next() unintentionally, or explicitly return next() in each branch. Recommended: compute progress, then have a single `return next();` at the end of the try, and `return next(error)` in catch. Delete the inline next() at line 266.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. The pre('save') hook calls next() at line 266 inside the if-branch (course found with modules) and again unconditionally at line 276 after the try block. On the happy path both fire, producing a genuine double-next() call. The else branch (line 267-270) only console.warn's and relies on the fall-through next() at 276. Mongoose double-next can trigger "next() called multiple times"/Overwrite errors and double-execute downstream middleware. Fix: remove the redundant next() at line 266 (the trailing one at 276 covers all branches), or restructure so each path calls next() exactly once. Severity high is slightly generous for a self-corrupting save-middleware bug — Mongoose largely tolerates duplicate next() (logs/throws but the save typically still completes), and the corruption is intermittent rather than guaranteed data loss; medium is more accurate.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: ID generation via countDocuments()+1 is racy and produces duplicate-key errors
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: Coach.coachId, Course.courseCode, and Assessment.assessmentCode are generated as PREFIX + (countDocuments()+1). Under concurrent creates two documents read the same count and generate the same code, causing E11000 duplicate-key failures (coachId/courseCode are unique). Also, if a document is ever deleted, count drops and a NEW doc reuses an existing code -> duplicate. User.js/Student.js/Teacher.js correctly use an atomic Counter via findByIdAndUpdate($inc); these three were not migrated.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Use the existing atomic Counter model pattern (as in User.js lines 136-150): `const counter = await Counter.findByIdAndUpdate({_id:'coachId'},{$inc:{seq:1}},{new:true,upsert:true}); this.coachId = 'CCH'+String(counter.seq).padStart(5,'0');` Apply the same to Course.courseCode and Assessment.assessmentCode.

verdict.note: Confirmed at all three referenced sites. Coach.js:63-69, Course.js:285-289, and Assessment.js:207-213 each generate their unique code in a pre('save') hook as PREFIX + padStart(countDocuments()+1): CCH/CRS/ASM. countDocuments() is a non-atomic read, so concurrent creates read the same count and produce identical codes -> E11000 on the unique index. Deleting any document also lowers the count, so a later insert reuses an existing code. The contrast claim is also accurate: User.js (139-141), Student.js (174-176), and Teacher.js (105-107) all import ./Counter and use Counter.findByIdAndUpdate({$inc:{seq:1}}) atomically, so these three models were indeed not migrated to the safe pattern. The inconsistency makes the bug and the intended fix unambiguous. Severity high is appropriate for production (duplicate-key failures under concurrency / after deletes block coach/course/assessment creation), though real-world impact depends on creation concurrency, which for an institute admin flow may be modest.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Registration password field is not select:false (sensitive field exposure)
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: Registration stores a bcrypt-hashed password (hashed in pre-save at line 226) but the field lacks `select:false`. Unlike User/Student/Teacher (which all use select:false), every default find()/findOne() on Registration returns the password hash, which can leak into API responses, logs, and JSON serialization. Registration also holds full PII (DOB, address, parent details) so accidental inclusion of the hash in admin list endpoints is a real exposure.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Add `select: false` to the password field: `password: { type: String, required: false, select: false }`. Audit any auth/login code that reads Registration.password and add `.select('+password')` where the hash is genuinely needed (e.g., comparePassword flow).

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. back-end/models/Registration.js:18 declares `password: { type: String, required: false }` with no `select:false`, and the pre-save hook (lines 226-235) bcrypt-hashes it. A grep for select:false on the password field in models found no match for Registration, confirming the asymmetry vs peer models. Real leak path exists: back-end/routes/users.js:824-826 returns `res.json({ ...registration.toObject(), ... })`, spreading the full document including the hashed password into the API response; registrations.js:67-75 is safe (uses explicit .select()), but the profile endpoint is not. The exposed value is a bcrypt hash (not plaintext), and the dump occurs on the account-owner profile fetch, so this is sensitive-data-exposure / defense-in-depth rather than direct credential compromise. Downgrading to medium: high overstates impact since a bcrypt hash alone does not grant authentication and is costly to brute-force.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Registration email and userId lack unique constraints and indexes
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: email (line 15) is `required` but NOT unique and NOT indexed; userId (line 5, ObjectId ref User) has no index/unique. This permits multiple Registration records for the same email/user, causing duplicate registrations and ambiguous lookups. Lookups by email/userId also do full collection scans. Other identity models (User/Student/Teacher) enforce unique email; Registration is the entry point yet has no such guard.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Add `unique: true, lowercase: true, index: true` to email (and a match validator consistent with other models). Add an index on userId, and decide whether one registration per user should be enforced (`registrationSchema.index({ userId: 1 }, { unique: true, sparse: true })`). At minimum: `registrationSchema.index({ email: 1 }, { unique: true });`.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. C:\Users\Vickram\Documents\SMAART\back-end\models\Registration.js line 5 `userId: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'User' }` has no `unique` and no `index`. Line 15 `email: { type: String, required: true }` is required but has neither `unique` nor `index`. No `schema.index(...)` calls exist anywhere in the file. So the factual basis of the claim is accurate: no uniqueness guard and no index on email/userId, meaning duplicate Registration records are possible at the DB level and email/userId lookups are unindexed (collection scans). Severity should be downgraded from high to medium: this is a data-integrity/performance concern, not a security vulnerability (no auth bypass, injection, or data exposure). Real-world impact is mitigated/conditional — controllers may enforce uniqueness via findOneAndUpdate/upsert before insert, the model supports progressive section saving (mobile/password optional), and impact on a registration collection that is typically small-to-moderate is limited. Adding a unique index on email (and an index on userId) is a reasonable hardening fix, but the absence is medium, not high.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: UserBadge has no unique index, allowing duplicate badge awards under concurrency
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: The award flow in badgeUtils.js does a non-atomic findOne({userId,badgeId,...}) then `new UserBadge(...).save()`. The only index on (userId,badgeId) is NON-unique (line 62: `userBadgeSchema.index({ userId: 1, badgeId: 1 })`). Two concurrent award requests (e.g. user finishing a module that triggers multiple badge checks, or double-clicked actions) both pass the findOne check and both insert, producing duplicate earned badges. This inflates XP, badge counts, and any denormalized totals derived from UserBadge.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Make the lookup key unique and atomic. Add `userBadgeSchema.index({ userId: 1, badgeId: 1 }, { unique: true })` (replacing the non-unique one) — or include the differentiator (metadata.moduleId/courseId) in a unique partial index if multiple instances per badge type are intended. Then change badgeUtils to use `UserBadge.findOneAndUpdate(query, { $setOnInsert: {...} }, { upsert: true, new: true })` and treat E11000 duplicate-key errors as 'already earned'. Backfill/dedupe existing duplicates before adding the unique index.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. UserBadge.js line 62 declares index({userId:1, badgeId:1}) with no unique:true; lines 63-64 are also non-unique. awardBadge in badgeUtils.js lines 28-48 performs a non-atomic findOne(query) then `new UserBadge(...).save()` with no transaction, upsert, or unique constraint, so two concurrent requests can both pass the isEarned check and both insert, producing duplicate earned badges that inflate XP (getUserBadgeStats sums xp over all earned, lines 183-196) and counts. One caveat: the actual dedupe key includes metadata.moduleId/courseId (lines 24-26), so a corrective unique index would need to span those fields, not just (userId,badgeId) — but the underlying race is real. Severity adjusted to medium: it is a gamification/XP-integrity correctness bug requiring concurrent or double-submit timing, affecting badge/XP stats only, not core security or critical data.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: exportToExcel does full file read-modify-write with no locking (race condition / data loss)
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: exportToExcel reads the entire workbook into memory, appends rows, and rewrites the whole file via XLSX.writeFile. The route POST /api/career-intelligence/export-excel calls this with no concurrency guard. Two concurrent (or rapid sequential) export requests both read the same baseline rows, each appends its own rows, and the last writer wins — silently dropping the other request's rows. Because the synchronous XLSX.writeFile is not awaited/queued, a crash mid-write can also truncate or corrupt the single shared file.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Serialize writes: introduce an in-process async mutex/queue around the read-modify-write, or write to a per-request/temp file then atomically rename. Better, persist exports to a database collection or append-only per-batch files instead of mutating one shared workbook. At minimum, wrap the read+append+write in a lock so concurrent exports cannot interleave.

verdict.note: Confirmed in back-end/services/excelExportService.js:29-104. exportToExcel reads the entire workbook (XLSX.readFile line 35, sheet_to_json line 38), appends new rows (push line 85), and rewrites the whole single shared file (XLSX.writeFile to module-level EXCEL_PATH, lines 11/91). There is no file lock, mutex, or write queue. The route POST /api/career-intelligence/export-excel (server.js:209) -> controller (careerSimulationController.js:453) invokes the synchronous service per request with no concurrency guard. Concurrent or rapid-sequential requests each read the same baseline rows and the last writeFile wins, silently dropping the other request's rows; a crash mid-writeFile can corrupt the shared file. The described mechanism is real. Severity calibration: this is an internal AI-agent output spreadsheet behind authMiddleware, not user-facing transactional data, so realistic blast radius is limited; I would rate it medium rather than high, but the bug genuinely exists.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: AddDetails passes wrong props to FileUpload, breaking 10th/12th marksheet upload

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: CoursePlayer calls undefined setIsCompleted() — crashes on 'Next Lesson'

The feature is non-functional. The claim about bypassing apiCall's auth/credentials handling is also accurate (raw fetch with only a Content-Type header). Note other handlers in the same file (handleSubmitRequest line 123, fetchMySessions line 75) correctly use apiCall, isolating the defect to this one function. Severity corrected from critical to high: it is a deterministic break, but scoped to a single secondary feature, is caught (no page crash / no data loss / no security impact), and degrades gracefully with an error toast — not the project-wide or data-integrity impact that "critical" implies.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Notifications fetchSummary calls undefined setSummary -> ReferenceError on every page load
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: fetchSummary() calls setSummary(data.summary) but there is no `summary` state declared (no `const [summary, setSummary] = useState(...)`). fetchSummary runs in a useEffect on mount (line 104-106). When the /notifications/summary call succeeds, setSummary is undefined and throws a ReferenceError inside the try, which is swallowed by the catch and logged as 'Error fetching summary'. The summary data is silently never stored. If the surrounding code is later refactored to use the value it will break; today it is dead/broken code that masks a real failure and wastes a network round-trip on every mount.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Either add the missing state `const [summary, setSummary] = useState(null);` near the other useState hooks if the summary is meant to be displayed, or delete the fetchSummary function, its useState-less setter, and the useEffect at lines 104-106 entirely if the summary panel was never built. Line 77 calls setSummary(data.summary), but no `const [summary, setSummary] = useState(...)` is declared anywhere in the component (only `filter` at L69 and `dateRange` at L70 exist), and setSummary is not destructured from useNotifications() (L56-67), imported, or defined locally. fetchSummary runs in a mount useEffect (L104-106). confirmedCriticalHigh.title: AdminTickets pagination Prev/Next use stale page due to setState+immediate fetch
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: The Previous/Next handlers call setPagination(prev => ({...prev, page: prev.page +/- 1})) and then synchronously call fetchTickets(). fetchTickets reads pagination.page from the current render's closure, which has NOT yet updated (setState is asynchronous). So the request is sent with the OLD page number while the UI label updates to the new page. Result: clicking Next shows 'page 2' in the footer but re-fetches page 1's data; the list and the page indicator disagree, and the user effectively cannot paginate. (Same stale-closure pattern affects the refresh button which is benign, but pagination is broken.)
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Pass the target page explicitly to fetchTickets instead of relying on state. E.g. give fetchTickets an optional page arg: `const fetchTickets = async (overridePage) => { const page = overridePage ?? pagination.page; ... }` and call `setPagination(p=>({...p,page:p.page+1})); fetchTickets(pagination.page+1);`. Better: drive fetching from a useEffect on pagination.page so it always fetches the committed value, and have the buttons only call setPagination.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. fetchTickets (line 66) reads pagination.page from the closure at line 72. The Prev/Next handlers (lines 358-377) call setPagination(prev => ...) then synchronously call fetchTickets() in the same closure, so the request is sent with the OLD page value (setState is async). Additionally, after the response, lines 84-88 reset pagination.page to response.pagination.page (the old page the server returned), overwriting the optimistic increment, so the page indicator reverts and the list never advances. There is no useEffect keyed on pagination.page to trigger a corrected refetch. Pagination is genuinely broken. Severity adjusted from high to medium: it is a real functional break but limited to UI navigation on an internal admin tickets page, with no security or data-integrity impact.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Model-loading gate in vision board editor resolves instantly — NSFW/toxicity checks run before models are ready
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: initModels() does `await Promise.all([loadToxicityModel(), preloadNSFWModel()])` then `setIsModelLoading(false)`. But preloadNSFWModel() (imageModeration.js:328) is NOT async — it fires `Promise.all([...]).catch()` internally and returns `undefined` synchronously. So the awaited Promise.all resolves as soon as the toxicity model loads (or immediately, since loadToxicityModel can also resolve fast), and isModelLoading is set to false while the NSFW.js + COCO-SSD models are still downloading in the background. The whole point of the `isModelLoading` flag and the 'Safety System Initializing' toast (handleSave line 1274) is defeated: a user can upload an image or hit Save in the first seconds and checkBase64ImageNSFW will lazy-load the model on the spot (slow first call) or, worse, the fail-open paths (handleImageUpload catch at line 541, checkNSFW catch returning {flagged:false}) silently admit unmoderated explicit content. This is a content-safety regression on a user-generated-content surface.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Make preloadNSFWModel return the promise so callers can await real readiness: `export const preloadNSFWModel = () => Promise.all([loadNSFWModel(), loadCocoModel()]);` (keep a `.catch` only at the call site). Then in initModels keep `await Promise.all([loadToxicityModel(), preloadNSFWModel()])` and only set isModelLoading false after both genuinely resolve. Additionally, in handleSave, when isModelLoading is still true do NOT just toast — `return` early (or `await` the model-ready promise) so an image is never saved before image moderation has run.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. VisionBoardEditorPro.jsx:218-228 does `await Promise.all([loadToxicityModel(), preloadNSFWModel()])` then `setIsModelLoading(false)`. imageModeration.js:328-336 defines `preloadNSFWModel = () => { Promise.all([loadNSFWModel(), loadCocoModel()]).catch(...) }` — a plain (non-async) function that fires the inner Promise.all without returning or awaiting it, so it returns `undefined` synchronously. Promise.all([...]) in the editor therefore only effectively waits on loadToxicityModel; the NSFW.js + COCO-SSD downloads continue in the background after isModelLoading flips to false. The gate behaviors are real too: handleSave (line 1274) only shows an 'initializing' toast and does NOT block/return — it continues saving regardless of isModelLoading. handleImageUpload (line 504) calls checkBase64ImageNSFW->checkImageComprehensive and its catch at line 541 fails open (admits the image with only a notification). So a user acting in the first seconds gets either a slow lazy-load on first call or, on error, silent fail-open admission of unmoderated content. The bug (missing `async`/`return` of the promise in preloadNSFWModel) is genuine. Severity high is appropriate but slightly aggravated/tempered: this is a UGC content-safety surface (justifies high), but exploitation requires acting within the model-download window AND the comprehensive check still runs on a slower lazy first call in the common (non-error) path — only the catch path is a true silent bypass. High is a fair rating.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: In-progress career report shows an infinite 'Generating' overlay — no polling for completion
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: On mount loadReports() reads sessionStorage 'generating_report_id'. If the tracked report exists but is neither 'completed' nor 'failed' (i.e. still generating server-side), it calls setIsGenerating(true) (line 82) — which renders the full-screen blocking overlay (lines 331-353) with the spinner and 'Mapping career data... / Running AI analysis...' steps. But there is NO polling loop or interval anywhere that re-checks the report status. The overlay therefore stays up forever; the user is locked out of the page until they manually reload, and even on reload the same branch re-triggers. The report may already be complete on the backend. This is a guaranteed stuck state for any report whose generation outlives the original request (the exact reason a tracking id is stored).
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: After setIsGenerating(true) for a still-pending tracked report, start a polling effect: a setInterval (e.g. every 5s, with a max attempt cap) that calls careerIntelligenceApi.getReports(), finds the tracked id, and on status 'completed' sets the report + clears the overlay + removes the sessionStorage key, on 'failed' sets the error + clears, and clears the interval on unmount. Also give the overlay a manual 'Cancel / Back' escape hatch so the user is never hard-locked.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. CareerDataFetcher.jsx line 82 calls setIsGenerating(true) when the tracked report (generating_report_id from sessionStorage) exists but is not 'completed'/'failed'. Lines 331-352 render isGenerating as a fixed inset-0 z-50 black/backdrop-blur full-screen blocking overlay with the exact 'Mapping career data... / Running AI analysis...' steps. There is no setInterval/setTimeout/polling anywhere in the file (verified by grep). loadReports runs once via the empty-dep useEffect (lines 116-119) and the only path that flips isGenerating back to false is handleSubmit's finally (line 189), which is never reached on mount. So the overlay stays up forever, and on reload the same branch re-triggers because the id is only removed on completed/failed (lines 76,80). Real, reproducible lockout. Severity: this requires a remount/refresh while a report is genuinely still generating server-side (the normal handleSubmit flow awaits and clears the id before finally), so it is conditional rather than guaranteed on every use — but that condition is precisely the case the tracking id was added to handle. Downgrading to medium: a full lockout but only in the deferred-generation timing window, recoverable conceptually though the code never recovers automatically.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Public certificate/passport verify pages fabricate fake 'Authenticated' results on the client
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: These are public verification endpoints (whole point: prove a credential is real). VerifyCertificate catches a 404 from the backend and, if the ID merely starts with 'SMAART-', builds a fully fabricated mockResponse with verified:true, a hard-coded studentId 'STU00006', readinessBand 'Proficient', and fake skills, then shows 'Certificate Authenticated Successfully'. VerifyPassport never calls the backend at all — it just sleeps 1.5s and returns verified:true for ANY id starting with 'SM-', pulling name/photo from URL query params (?name=&photo=) and localStorage. An attacker can forge a green 'Certified Authentic' / 'Passport Authentic' screen for any name simply by crafting a URL or ID, completely defeating the verification feature and enabling credential fraud.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Remove all client-side mock/demo fallbacks. VerifyCertificate: on a 404 (or non-success) show the 'not found' error — never synthesize verified:true. VerifyPassport: replace the setTimeout/startsWith('SM-') simulation with a real apiCall('/passports/verify/:id') and render strictly from the server's verified flag. Never trust query-param name/photo/institution or localStorage for displaying a 'verified' identity; render only fields the backend returns.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. VerifyCertificate.jsx:110-163 catches a 404 and, if certId starts with 'SMAART-', builds mockResponse with verified:true, hard-coded studentId 'STU00006', readinessBand 'Proficient', and fabricated validatedSkills, then renders an authenticated result (toast labeled 'Demo Mode'). VerifyPassport.jsx:51-133 makes NO backend call at all — the apiCall is commented out (lines 62-63); it setTimeout(1500) then returns verified:true for ANY id starting with 'SM-', pulling name/photo/institution from URL query params (location.search ?name=/?photo=) and localStorage. VerifyPassport is the cleanly exploitable one: unauthenticated, no server check, name fully attacker-controlled via ?name=. VerifyCertificate's path requires a 404 from the real backend and derives the name from the logged-in user (defaulting to 'Verified Student'), so it cannot set an arbitrary victim name via that path, but still fabricates an authenticated screen. Both defeat the verification feature. Severity critical is appropriate: these are the public credential-verification endpoints whose sole purpose is fraud prevention.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Hard-coded http:// API base URL — breaks under HTTPS and is insecure in production
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: getApiBaseUrl()/getBackendUrl() force 'http://${hostname}:5000' for any non-localhost host, and even the localhost branch defaults to http. In production (HTTPS), this generates mixed-content requests the browser blocks, so every API call fails; it also sends the Bearer token and session cookies over plaintext http. The hard-coded :5000 port also assumes the API is co-located on that port, which is rarely true behind a reverse proxy / on a deployed domain.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Drive the base URL entirely from VITE_API_URL (e.g. 'https://api.smaart.example/api') in all environments, falling back to a relative '/api' path that inherits the page's protocol/host when the env var is absent. Remove the hard-coded protocol and :5000 port. Never downgrade to http for authenticated calls.

verdict.note: Confirmed in front-end/src/services/api.js. getApiBaseUrl() (line 12) and getBackendUrl() (line 27) hard-code `http://${hostname}:5000` for any non-localhost host with no HTTPS path and no env override on that branch; the localhost branch (lines 9, 25) also defaults to http (though it allows VITE_API_URL). Under an HTTPS production domain this yields mixed-content (browser-blocked) requests and sends the Bearer token over plaintext, and the fixed :5000 assumes a co-located port rather than a reverse proxy. All claimed facts are present in the code. Severity adjusted to medium: the impact is real but entirely contingent on an HTTPS production deployment, whereas the file is explicitly built for LAN/network-IP dev access (per its header comment); it is a deployment/design defect, not an exploitable runtime vuln in the intended LAN use, so medium is more defensible than high.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Live production secrets committed to git (MongoDB Atlas creds, JWT secret, Cloudinary, SMTP, OpenRouter, Deepgram, ITSM keys)
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: back-end/.env and back-end/.env.backup are tracked in the repository and contain REAL, working credentials: MongoDB Atlas connection string with embedded username/password (souban:souban123) granting full DB read/write with authSource=admin; a 256-bit JWT_SECRET (forging this lets anyone mint valid auth tokens for any user/admin); Cloudinary API secret; a Gmail SMTP app password (SMTP_PASS=hhpc xyxl petg vdls); OPENROUTER_API_KEY; DEEPGRAM_API_KEY; ITSM_API_KEY; plus hardcoded backdoor-style constants ADMIN_SYSTEM_SECRET=smaart-admin-bypass-2026 and USERDASHBOARD_SYNC_TOKEN=sync-dashboard-secret-2026. The contents match every claimed secret: MONGODB_URI with embedded souban:souban123 and authSource=admin (full Atlas DB access); a 64-hex-char JWT_SECRET usable to forge auth tokens; CLOUDINARY_API_SECRET; Gmail SMTP_PASS=hhpc xyxl petg vdls (app password); OPENROUTER_API_KEY (sk-or-v1-...); DEEPGRAM_API_KEY; ITSM_API_KEY; ADMIN_SYSTEM_SECRET=smaart-admin-bypass-2026 and USERDASHBOARD_SYNC_TOKEN=sync-dashboard-secret-2026. But the running code and the secrets template use OPENROUTER_API_KEY (the actual AI provider per .env line 22-24, OPENAI_API_KEY is not in .env), OPENROUTER_BASE_URL, AI_MODEL, SMTP_USER/SMTP_PASS/SMTP_HOST (SES), DEEPGRAM_API_KEY, ITSM_API_KEY, USERDASHBOARD_SYNC_TOKEN, ADMIN_SYSTEM_SECRET, and REDIS_USERNAME. confirmedCriticalHigh.title: MongoDB Atlas reachable from entire VPC CIDR and via NAT public IP; connection string uses admin auth
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: The Atlas IP access list is configured to whitelist the whole 10.0.0.0/16 VPC CIDR plus the NAT Gateway Elastic IP. Whitelisting the NAT EIP means Atlas is reachable from any host that egresses through that NAT (and the EIP is internet-facing), weakening the 'private only' claim. The leaked production connection string also authenticates as an admin-source user (authSource=admin) with a weak password, and the example string keeps public 0.0.0.0/0 guidance only as a 'remove' note.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Use Atlas Private Endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) or VPC peering ONLY, and remove the NAT EIP and broad CIDR entries from the Atlas IP access list so the DB is never reachable from the public internet. Create a dedicated least-privilege Atlas database user scoped to the smaartminds DB (readWrite on that DB only, not authSource=admin), with a strong rotated password stored in Secrets Manager. Enforce TLS (ssl=true) which the string already has. Enable Atlas auditing and network access logging.

verdict.note: Both referenced lines exist. security-policies.md:90-97 does whitelist the full 10.0.0.0/16 VPC CIDR plus the NAT Gateway EIP, and .env:3 contains a live Atlas connection string with weak password 'souban123' and authSource=admin. BUT the finding conflates two unequal things. The NAT-EIP/whole-CIDR critique is advisory markdown guidance describing intended hardening (it also recommends VPC Peering and removing 0.0.0.0/0); it is a defensible design nit, not an exploitable code misconfiguration. The actually serious part is the committed Atlas admin credential in .env with a trivial password — a real secret-exposure issue (alongside other leaked secrets: Cloudinary, OpenRouter, Deepgram, SMTP app password, JWT_SECRET). The title inflates a doc-quality critique by bundling it with the real .env leak. Real, but the headline 'high' rests mainly on the design critique; corrected to medium with the .env credential exposure being the genuine concern.

confirmedCriticalHigh.title: Raw WebSocket and Socket.io auth pass JWT in URL query string; tokens land in ALB/CloudWatch access logs
confirmedCriticalHigh.description: Both the raw ws upgrade (`url.parse(req.url, true).query.token`) and the socket.io handshake accept the JWT via query string. The deployment terminates TLS at the ALB and forwards to targets; ALB access logs, CloudWatch, proxies, and browser history will capture the full URL including the bearer token, leaking long-lived credentials. Combined with the leaked JWT_SECRET this is especially severe, but it is a problem regardless. There is also no token-expiry / re-auth handling on long-lived sockets.
confirmedCriticalHigh.fix: Authenticate websockets via the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header or an Authorization header / httpOnly cookie rather than the query string, and disable ALB query-string logging or scrub tokens. Verify token expiry on connect and periodically re-validate (close the socket when the JWT expires) rather than trusting an indefinitely-open connection. Rotate JWT_SECRET (see secrets finding) so previously-logged tokens become invalid.

verdict.note: Confirmed in code. Raw ws upgrade (lines 155-156) reads `url.parse(req.url, true).query.token` and passes it to getUserIdFromToken. Socket.io middleware (lines 107-109) accepts `socket.handshake.query?.token` as a fallback auth source. Both place the JWT in the URL query string, which is captured in ALB access logs, CloudWatch, intermediary proxies, and browser history — a real credential-leakage vector. Mitigating nuance: both paths ALSO accept the token via safer channels (socket.io: handshake.auth.token and Authorization header; raw ws clients typically can't set headers in browsers, so query string is often the only browser-side option for native WebSocket). The query-string acceptance is opt-in by the client, not forced, but since it is offered and clients (especially browser WebSocket) will use it, the logging-exposure risk is genuine. No token-expiry/re-auth on long-lived sockets is also accurate — auth happens once at connect and is never re-checked. Severity high is slightly aggressive for a standalone finding (query-string token logging is a well-known medium-tier issue), but given the description references a separately-leaked JWT_SECRET (forgeable long-lived tokens) the elevated rating is defensible. Rating as high.

refuted.title: Authenticated mutation/upload fetch calls omit the Authorization header
refuted.description: These pages call protected endpoints (/users/register-section PATCH, /upload POST) with a raw `fetch()` that sends only `{ 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }` and no `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header and no `credentials: 'include'`. The GET calls in the same files (Profile.jsx:319, Settings.jsx:64) DO attach the token, proving the API expects it. As a result every profile/settings save, certificate add/delete, and photo/file upload will be rejected (401) or processed unauthenticated. The handlers only check `response.ok`, so on a 401 the user sees a generic 'Failed to save' / 'Failed to upload' toast with no session-expiry handling or redirect.
refuted.fix: Route all of these through the shared `apiCall` from @/services/api (which injects auth headers, credentials, 401 handling, and timeout) instead of raw fetch. If raw fetch must stay, add `credentials: 'include'` and `Authorization: \`Bearer ${sessionStorage.getItem('token')}\`` consistently, and handle 401 explicitly.

verdict.note: The frontend code observations are accurate: Profile.jsx (lines 187, 220, 281, 461, 469, 522, 548, 589) and Settings.jsx (lines 101, 139) all issue PATCH /users/register-section and POST /upload with no Authorization header and no credentials:'include', while the GET at Profile.jsx:319 and Settings.jsx:64-65 does attach a Bearer token. However the finding's core CLAIM and predicted impact are FALSE. The backend route handler `router.patch('/register-section', async (req,res) => ...)` at back-end/routes/users.js:413 has NO auth middleware, and `router.post('/', ...)` in back-end/routes/uploadRoutes.js:10 has only a rate limiter (generalLimiter) and NO auth. So these endpoints do NOT require a token and will NOT return 401 — the saves/uploads succeed unauthenticated. The premise 'GET attaching a token proves the API expects it' is invalid: the GET attaches a token but the mutation endpoints don't enforce one. Thus 'every profile/settings save will be rejected (401)' is incorrect; the feature works. The actual real problem is the inverse — these mutation endpoints are unauthenticated on the server (broken access control / IDOR: any caller can PATCH any user's record by passing an arbitrary email), which the repo's own notes (full_commits.md: 'backend must enforce auth here') acknowledge. That is a genuine vuln but is a different finding from the one claimed. As stated (functional breakage via 401), the finding is refuted.

refuted.title: Dockerfile bakes entire source tree and dev/native build toolchain into the runtime image
refuted.description: The runner stage does `COPY --from=builder /usr/src/app ./` which copies the ENTIRE build context (`COPY . .` in the builder). Because there is no build artifact to separate, the multi-stage split provides almost no size or secret benefit - all source, configs, and crucially any committed back-end/.env / .env.backup get baked into the production image layers. The build also installs python3, make, g++, git (line 8) which are unnecessary at runtime and enlarge attack surface. The Dockerfile relies on .dockerignore (referenced in a comment) to exclude .env, but .dockerignore is not shown/guaranteed and the committed .env would otherwise be shipped inside the container.
refuted.fix: Verify a .dockerignore exists at the build-context root that excludes .env, .env.*, .git, node_modules, tests, docs, front-end. Since this is a pure Node app with no compile step, drop the build toolchain from the runtime stage entirely (only install python3/make/g++ in builder if native modules truly need them, then discard). Copy only required runtime files (node_modules, server.js, the back-end source dirs) explicitly rather than the whole tree. Pin the base image by digest (node:20-alpine@sha256:...) rather than a mutable tag. Confirm no secret files are present in the final image via `docker history` / image scan.

verdict.note: The finding's central claims are refuted by the actual code. (1) Secret leakage: a .dockerignore DOES exist at aws-deployment/.dockerignore and explicitly excludes .env, .env.backup, *.env, *.pem, *.key, credentials.json, .git/, front-end/, tests/, etc. The finding speculated the .dockerignore was "not shown/guaranteed" — it is present and comprehensive, so committed back-end/.env / .env.backup would NOT be baked into the image. (2) Dev/native toolchain in runtime: python3/make/g++/git are installed via `apk add` on line 8, which is in the BUILDER stage only (FROM ... AS builder). The runner stage (line 20, FROM node:20-alpine AS runner) starts from a fresh base and only does `COPY --from=builder` of node_modules and app files — it does NOT inherit the builder's apk-installed packages. So the toolchain is correctly discarded and is NOT in the production runtime image; this is exactly what the multi-stage split achieves. The only literally-true sliver is that `COPY . .` copies the whole context and the multi-stage size benefit is modest for a non-compiled Node app — but that is normal/benign, not a high-severity security issue, and even then is bounded by the .dockerignore exclusions. The finding mischaracterizes the runtime attack surface and the secret risk.

refuted.title: India DPDP Act 2023 data-residency, processor obligations, and third-party transfers not addressed
refuted.description: The platform processes personal data of Indian data principals (students/users: resumes, profiles, career data, images). Under the DPDP Act 2023, SMAART is a Data Fiduciary with obligations: lawful consent, purpose limitation, security safeguards, breach notification to the Data Protection Board, and data-principal rights (access/correction/erasure). Several deployment choices create compliance gaps: (1) AI processing routes user data to OpenRouter/OpenAI and OCR/NSFW services whose servers are typically OUTSIDE India - cross-border transfer is permitted under DPDP only to non-restricted countries and requires contractual safeguards and is not documented here; (2) Cloudinary stores user-uploaded images/resumes - storage region/residency is not pinned to India; (3) MongoDB Atlas region/residency is unspecified in the deploy docs (the leaked URI's cluster region is not clearly India); (4) the committed-secret breach itself is a reportable security failure; (5) there is no data retention/erasure mechanism evident for notifications, logs (CloudWatch retains forever by default), and uploads.
refuted.fix: Map all personal-data flows and document them. Keep primary data stores in India: pin MongoDB Atlas to an AWS India region and Cloudinary to an India storage region (or self-host media in S3 ap-south-1). For AI/OCR vendors that process abroad, execute DPDP-compliant data processing agreements, minimize/anonymize data sent (do not send raw PII to third-party LLMs unnecessarily), and confirm none are in a government-restricted country. Set CloudWatch log retention (e.g. 30-90 days) and ensure logs do not capture PII or tokens. Implement data-principal rights (export/erase) across MongoDB, Cloudinary, Redis, and backups. Maintain a breach-response process and report the already-leaked-secrets incident as required. Enable encryption at rest (Atlas, ElastiCache, ECR already AES256, S3, CloudWatch via KMS) and document consent capture in the app.

verdict.note: Refuted on the code. The referenced files are a `.example` template plus an ECS task definition; both use placeholders and AWS Secrets Manager ARNs — there is NO leaked/committed secret (the claim's premise (4) and references to "the leaked URI's cluster region" are fabricated). The env header explicitly warns never to commit real credentials. Infra is consistently pinned to India's ap-south-1 (Mumbai): CloudWatch logs region, every Secrets Manager ARN, and SMTP host email-smtp.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com; the MongoDB URI shows a region placeholder, undercutting the "residency unspecified" point. The remaining DPDP items (cross-border AI transfers to OpenAI/OpenRouter, Cloudinary region not pinned, no documented retention/erasure) are legal/compliance/documentation governance gaps, not code defects — and CloudWatch "retains forever" is not set anywhere in code. Not a verifiable code vulnerability.

mediumLow.title: Account enumeration in signup, login (cross-college), and forgot-password
mediumLow.description: Multiple endpoints reveal account existence. send-signup-otp returns 'An account with this email already exists' (auth.js:93). Login returns a distinct message 'This account belongs to a different institution' when the email exists in another college (auth.js:463). forgot-password, despite a comment claiming non-disclosure and a generic success message, actually returns 404 'No account found with this email address' / 'Email not found at this institution' (auth.js:1080,1099) — directly confirming whether an email is registered, defeating the generic message at line 1129.
mediumLow.fix: Return uniform responses regardless of account existence. For forgot-password, always return the generic 'If an account exists...' 200 response and never a 404 that reveals existence. For login, use one generic 'Invalid credentials' message. Signup-OTP enumeration is harder to fully avoid but can be reduced by sending an email either way and returning a uniform response.

mediumLow.title: Login flow lacks failed-password attempt lockout (account lockout only triggers on OTP, after password already verified)
mediumLow.description: Password verification (bcrypt.compare at 505/519) has no per-account failed-attempt counter or lockout — checkAccountLock only reads accountLockedUntil, which is set only by the OTP flow (auth.js:793). loginLimiter provides some throttling but is typically IP-based; an attacker rotating IPs or behind shared NAT can brute-force passwords because failed password attempts neither increment a counter nor lock the account. The account lock comment at line 482 ('Check account lock BEFORE password verification') is misleading since nothing in the password path ever sets the lock.
mediumLow.fix: Track failed password attempts on the user record and set accountLockedUntil after N failures (mirroring the OTP lockout). Apply the lock check and increment for all user types, not just students. Ensure loginLimiter is keyed appropriately and consider an account-scoped limiter in addition to IP-scoped.

mediumLow.title: resend-login-otp and resend-signup-otp have no rate limiting / cooldown enforcement (email bombing)
mediumLow.description: POST /resend-login-otp is registered with only the router-level generalLimiter — no otpLimiter or passwordResetLimiter and no use of the defined OTP_RESEND_COOLDOWN constant (auth.js:25, which is never referenced anywhere). An attacker who has a valid tempToken can repeatedly call resend to send unlimited OTP emails to the victim (email bombing) and regenerate tokens. resend-signup-otp uses passwordResetLimiter but similarly ignores the cooldown.
mediumLow.fix: Apply a strict limiter (e.g. otpLimiter) to resend-login-otp, and enforce the OTP_RESEND_COOLDOWN by checking lastOtpSentAt before issuing a new OTP, returning 429 if within the cooldown window.

mediumLow.title: verify-reset-otp / reset-password lack rate limiting and a strong attempt cap, enabling OTP brute force
mediumLow.description: POST /verify-reset-otp and POST /reset-password are not wrapped in passwordResetLimiter/otpLimiter (only the global generalLimiter applies). They allow up to 5 attempts (auth.js:1154,1204) but on hitting the cap they merely delete the OTP and ask the user to request a new one — combined with the unthrottled forgot-password flow, an attacker can loop request->guess to brute-force the numeric OTP. The OTP space (6 digits) is small enough that without strict global throttling this is feasible.
mediumLow.fix: Apply otpLimiter to verify-reset-otp and reset-password keyed by resetToken/IP. Reduce attempts, add exponential backoff, and ensure forgot-password cannot be called repeatedly to refresh tokens without cooldown. Consider increasing OTP entropy.

mediumLow.title: Signup OTP record is never deleted after successful verification (replayable verification state)
mediumLow.description: verify-signup-otp marks the record isUsed=true but does not delete it, and the subsequent registration step trusts a client-supplied email/fullName rather than the verified record. Because /register (auth.js:234) does not consult the verified LoginOtp at all, a caller can skip verify-signup-otp entirely and register any email — the OTP email-verification gate is not actually enforced at account creation.
mediumLow.fix: Bind registration to a verified signup token: in /register require the tempToken from a verified account-verify LoginOtp whose userData.email matches the registration email, then consume (delete) it. Reject registration if no verified token exists.

mediumLow.title: Single-session check is bypassable because login JWTs (24h) without sessionId are still accepted by protect
mediumLow.description: The initial /register (auth.js:287) and the pre-OTP /login JWT (auth.js:612) are signed WITHOUT a sessionId and with 24h expiry. In protect (auth.js:78) the single-session and 3-hour-expiry checks only run `if (decoded.sessionId)`. A token lacking sessionId therefore skips session invalidation and the hard expiry wall entirely. The /register endpoint hands out such a 24h sessionId-less token directly, so a registered user holds a long-lived token immune to logout/kick/session-expiry enforcement.
mediumLow.fix: Do not issue usable auth JWTs before OTP/session establishment; the /register token should not grant access to protected resources. In protect, treat the absence of sessionId on a user that has session enforcement enabled as invalid (require sessionId for all authenticated access), or stop issuing sessionId-less tokens anywhere.

mediumLow.title: Reset-password uses bcrypt cost factor 10 while ignoring model pre-save hashing — inconsistent and low work factor
mediumLow.description: reset-password manually does bcrypt.hash(newPassword, 10) and writes the hash directly, whereas other flows rely on the model pre-save hook. Cost factor 10 is below the currently recommended 12 for bcrypt, and bypassing the model hook risks divergence if the model uses a different cost or additional logic. Mixed hashing paths make rotation/upgrades error-prone.
mediumLow.fix: Centralize password hashing in the model pre-save hook (assign student.password = newPassword and save) rather than hashing inline, and raise the bcrypt cost factor to at least 12 in one place. Ensure all reset/change flows use the same path.

mediumLow.title: verifyAssessmentToken trusts client-supplied resultId and only checks when present; no DB ownership check
mediumLow.description: The token mismatch check only runs `if (bodyResultId)` — if the route reads resultId from elsewhere or omits it, the binding is skipped and any valid assessment token is accepted. The user-match check only runs `if (req.user)`, so on routes where this middleware runs without protect first, req.user is undefined and the user binding is silently skipped, allowing a token issued for one user to be used by another.
mediumLow.fix: Always require and validate resultId against decoded.resultId (reject if absent). Ensure protect runs before verifyAssessmentToken so req.user is always present, and make the user-match check mandatory (reject when req.user is missing). Optionally re-validate result ownership against the DB.

mediumLow.title: deviceFingerprint captures req.ip but app likely lacks trust proxy, making IP spoofable / inaccurate
mediumLow.description: The fingerprint relies on req.ip and req.headers['user-agent'], both client-influenced. If any session binding later trusts these values for security decisions, they are trivially spoofable (User-Agent is fully attacker-controlled; req.ip behind a proxy without app.set('trust proxy') reflects the proxy, and with naive XFF handling can be spoofed). As written it is informational only, but binding sessions to it would create a false sense of security.
mediumLow.fix: Do not use User-Agent/IP as a security boundary for session binding. If used for anomaly detection only, document that. Ensure 'trust proxy' is configured correctly so req.ip is the real client IP, and never derive authorization decisions from these values.

mediumLow.title: Registration upload Cloudinary folder derived from unauthenticated request body email
mediumLow.description: registrationStorage builds the Cloudinary folder from req.body.email with .replace(/[^a-zA-Z0-9]/g,'_'). Because /api/upload has no auth, an attacker fully controls the folder path. While special chars are stripped (so true path traversal into other Cloudinary trees is blocked), an attacker can write into ANY user's registration folder by supplying that user's email (registrations/<victim_email>), polluting/overwriting nobody's files but enabling spoofing of another user's uploaded documents and reconnaissance of the namespace. There is no binding to the authenticated user.
mediumLow.fix: Derive the folder from req.user._id (the authenticated user), as dynamicStorage already does, not from req.body.email. Never trust client-supplied identifiers for storage paths.

mediumLow.title: Unauthenticated, SSRF-capable OCR/NSFW endpoints accepting arbitrary image data
mediumLow.description: POST /api/ocr/extract and POST /api/nsfw/check are unauthenticated (only generalLimiter). imageData is forwarded to third-party APIs. In nsfwModeration the imageData is placed directly into image_url.url; if a remote URL (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/...) is supplied instead of base64, the downstream model provider may fetch it server-side (SSRF via the LLM's image fetcher) and the content is logged. Both endpoints are also free proxies for OCR/AI cost amplification.
mediumLow.fix: Require authentication (protect) on both routes. Validate that imageData is strictly base64 (or a data: URI) and reject anything matching ^https?:// before forwarding. Enforce a max payload size. Remove the verbose console.log of imageData/raw results.

mediumLow.title: NSFW moderation fails open on every error and weak parse fallback
mediumLow.description: scanImage returns isSafe:true when the API key is missing, on empty response, on JSON parse failure (keyword fallback only catches the exact substring '"issafe": false'), and on ANY thrown error (timeout, 4xx/5xx). An attacker can reliably bypass moderation by forcing a timeout (oversized image, slow upload) or by making the model return prose instead of strict JSON. Combined with uploads not being scanned at all (uploadRoutes), explicit/violent imagery can be stored and served from your Cloudinary domain.
mediumLow.fix: Fail closed for security-relevant moderation: on error/timeout/missing-key, reject the upload (or quarantine for manual review) rather than returning isSafe:true. Treat unparseable model output as unsafe. Actually invoke scanImage from the upload pipeline before persisting to Cloudinary.

mediumLow.title: Stored arbitrary URL accepted for user certificate (stored XSS / phishing vector)
mediumLow.description: POST /api/user-certificates accepts req.body.certificateUrl and verificationUrl unchecked and stores them as the certificate's URL. A user can store javascript:, data:, or attacker-controlled http URLs that are later rendered/linked in the UI, enabling stored XSS or phishing when other users (or admins) view the certificate. No scheme/host allowlist is applied.
mediumLow.fix: Validate certificateUrl/verificationUrl against an allowlist of schemes (https only) and, ideally, an allowlist of trusted hosts (your Cloudinary domain). Reject javascript:/data:/relative payloads. Ensure the frontend renders these as text/escaped href with rel=noopener and never via dangerouslySetInnerHTML.

mediumLow.title: Resume content fingerprint uses non-cryptographic FNV hash truncated for public IDs
mediumLow.description: buildResumeFingerprint uses a 32-bit FNV-1a variant (hashString) producing only ~7 base36 chars. This is the sole integrity check behind the public QR verification (routes/resumes.js verify endpoint compares record.fingerprint === supplied h). A 32-bit non-cryptographic hash is trivially collidable, so a tampered resume can be crafted to produce the same fingerprint and pass 'content fingerprint matches' verification, defeating the anti-forgery purpose. createResumePublicId further uses only fingerprint.slice(0,4) plus 4 random bytes.
mediumLow.fix: Use a keyed cryptographic hash (HMAC-SHA256 with a server secret) over the canonical resume JSON for the fingerprint, and store/compare the full digest. Do not derive the public ID from the fingerprint prefix; use crypto.randomBytes for the unguessable component only.

mediumLow.title: x-forwarded-for trusted blindly for stored client IP
mediumLow.description: getClientIp reads the first value of the client-controlled X-Forwarded-For header and stores it in exportHistory[].ip. An attacker can spoof arbitrary IPs in the audit log, undermining the integrity of export tracking used for abuse investigation.
mediumLow.fix: Configure app.set('trust proxy', <known proxy count/CIDR>) and rely on req.ip, or validate XFF only when the request originates from a trusted proxy. Do not use raw header for security-relevant logging.

mediumLow.title: fileFilter relies on client MIME type plus extension, no magic-byte/content validation
mediumLow.description: All multer fileFilters accept a file when the client-supplied file.mimetype AND the filename extension are in the allowlist. Both are attacker-controlled, so a malicious payload (e.g. a polyglot or an HTML/SVG file) renamed to .jpg with Content-Type image/jpeg passes. For the registration storage, PDFs are stored as Cloudinary resource_type 'raw', meaning the original bytes are served verbatim from your Cloudinary domain with no transformation/sanitization (image uploads get re-encoded by the transformation, which mitigates them, but raw PDFs do not).
mediumLow.fix: Validate actual file content (magic bytes via file-type/ sharp re-encode for images). For PDFs served as raw, set Content-Disposition: attachment and serve from a separate non-app domain, or sanitize/render server-side. Do not trust client mimetype as the security boundary.

mediumLow.title: Self-vote/like protection bypassable; voting/reporting trust client userId
mediumLow.description: These handlers fall back to `req.body.userId` when req.user is absent and only block self-interaction when `actorRole === 'student'`. A user can inflate their own post's quality/likes by sending a different `userId`, or stuff poll/peer votes for arbitrary user ids (poll vote at 1558 and bookmark at 1502 use the raw body userId with no req.user fallback at all). Report dedup (line 1285) keys off body userId, so the same actor can report repeatedly under different ids. This corrupts qualityScore, leaderboard points, and the moderation flag pipeline.
mediumLow.fix: Use `const actorId = (req.user._id).toString()` and remove the `|| userId` body fallback in all of these handlers. Drop the role-conditional and always block self-voting/liking. Key report/vote dedup on the authenticated user id.

mediumLow.title: Group membership endpoints allow non-members to join arbitrary groups and trust client userId
mediumLow.description: POST /community/groups/:id/membership takes `userId` and `action` from the body and pushes that arbitrary userId into group.members with no check that it equals req.user, no college-scope check, and no membership/privacy enforcement — an authenticated user can add any user id to any group, or join private/other-college groups. This bypasses the college-scoping and admin-invite model that the parallel groups.js router (e.g. /:id/members at groups.js:185) carefully enforces.
mediumLow.fix: Use req.user._id as the only member id. Enforce group.isPublic / college scoping before allowing self-join, and reject join requests for private groups unless invited by an admin. Mirror the authorization model used in routes/groups.js.

mediumLow.title: WebSocket auth accepts token from query string, logging tokens and bypassing httpOnly
mediumLow.description: Both the socket.io middleware and the raw ws upgrade accept the JWT from the query string (`socket.handshake.query.token`, `url.parse(req.url,true).query.token`). Tokens in query strings are routinely written to access logs, proxy logs, and browser history, and survive Referer leakage — increasing the chance of token theft and session hijacking of the notification channel. The socket.io CORS config also uses `origin: true` with `credentials: true` (line 25-28), reflecting any Origin, which weakens cross-origin protections for the realtime channel.
mediumLow.fix: Accept the token only from the `auth` payload (socket.handshake.auth.token) or the Authorization header for socket.io; for the raw ws upgrade prefer a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`/header-based token rather than the URL. Replace `origin: true` with an explicit allowlist of trusted front-end origins. Consider verifying the user's current session/suspension status at connect time, not just signature validity.

mediumLow.title: NoSQL operator injection via unsanitized query params in escalations and ticket filters
mediumLow.description: Filter values from req.query are assigned directly into Mongo query objects (`query.student = student`, `query.status = status`, `query.userId = userId`, etc.). Express parses `?status[$ne]=x` into an object, so unless a body/query sanitizer (express-mongo-sanitize) is globally applied, an attacker can inject operators — e.g. `GET /api/tickets/all?userId[$ne]=000...` returns all users' tickets, or escalations filters can be turned into operator objects to exfiltrate beyond intended scope. The escalations case is especially severe because that router has no auth at all.
mediumLow.fix: Coerce all filter params to strings before use (`String(status)`), or validate against enumerations with express-validator, and apply express-mongo-sanitize globally to strip `$`/`.` keys from req.query and req.body. For tickets/all, this is defense-in-depth on top of the existing admin check.

mediumLow.title: Notification broadcast emails entire student body with unescaped admin-controlled content and no rate limit
mediumLow.description: POST /notifications/broadcast (admin-gated) and announcement creation fan out to every active student via insertMany + per-student email in setImmediate with title/message taken verbatim from the request. There is no length cap or content sanitization, and email rendering (sendSystemAnnouncementEmail / announcement notifications) interpolates these strings. A compromised or careless admin/college_admin can inject HTML into thousands of emails or trigger a heavy synchronous-per-student email loop (DoS / mail-reputation risk). Announcements POST is reachable by college_admin, widening the blast radius.
mediumLow.fix: Validate and cap title/message length, HTML-escape before email rendering, and move bulk email to a queued/batched worker with throttling rather than an in-request loop. Confirm role checks are sufficient for the volume of recipients each role can reach.

mediumLow.title: Poll JSON.parse on user input can crash the request and stored poll/sharedPost fields are unvalidated
mediumLow.description: In POST /discussions, `JSON.parse(req.body.poll)` runs on raw user input with no try/catch around just that parse; malformed JSON throws and is only caught by the outer handler returning a generic 500 (poor UX, and the parse happens after NSFW/cloudinary work, wasting resources). In groups share-post, the entire `postData` object (title, content, author, media, poll) is taken from the client and stored as a message verbatim with no membership-scoped validation that the referenced discussion exists or that the author/media are legitimate — enabling spoofed 'shared post' content (including arbitrary media URLs) inside group chats.
mediumLow.fix: Wrap the poll parse in its own try/catch returning 400 on invalid JSON, and validate poll shape (question string, options array bounds). For share-post, look up the real CommunityPost by discussionId server-side and build the sharedPost snapshot from the trusted document instead of trusting client postData.

mediumLow.title: Public debug endpoint dumps entire course catalog before auth
mediumLow.description: GET /api/courses/debug-flashcards-db is registered BEFORE router.use(protect) (line 74), so it is fully public. It runs Course.find({}) and returns flashcard content and metadata for every course with no pagination, leaking proprietary content and enabling a cheap DoS by loading all courses.
mediumLow.fix: Remove this debug endpoint from production, or move it below router.use(protect) and gate it behind authorize('admin'). Add pagination/limits if retained.

mediumLow.title: Admin bypass header trusts NODE_ENV and a shared secret
mediumLow.description: protect grants full admin (role:'admin') to any request sending x-admin-bypass:true plus x-admin-secret matching ADMIN_SYSTEM_SECRET whenever NODE_ENV !== 'production'. If NODE_ENV is unset/misconfigured in any deployed environment (staging, container without explicit env), this becomes a complete authentication bypass. The bypassed user also gets a random throwaway _id, so any ownership checks based on it are meaningless.
mediumLow.fix: Remove the bypass entirely, or guard it behind an explicit allowlisted flag (e.g. ENABLE_ADMIN_BYPASS === 'true') that is never set in any shared/deployed environment, and ensure NODE_ENV is always explicitly 'production' in prod deployment configs. Audit deployment manifests to confirm NODE_ENV is set.

mediumLow.title: PII (full profile incl. name/email) sent to third-party LLMs without consent gate or minimization
mediumLow.description: Resume generation sends the user's real fullName, education, institution, and experience to OpenRouter (a third-party broker that may route to free/community models — default model is 'meta-llama/llama-3.2-3b-instruct:free', openRouterService.js:11). answerCareerQuestion sends the entire JSON.stringify(userProfile) which can include name, currentRole, goals. enhanceWithAI sends degree/specialisation/skills to Anthropic. There is no PII-minimization or user-consent boundary, and free-tier OpenRouter models have weaker data-handling guarantees. For an Indian education platform this is a real privacy/DPDP exposure.
mediumLow.fix: Minimize PII sent to the LLM: omit or pseudonymize full name and email where not strictly required (the resume can re-insert the name client-side after generation), and never send the full JSON.stringify(userProfile). Pin a paid model with a contractual no-training data policy instead of the ':free' default, document the third-party processing, and add an explicit user consent/opt-in for AI features.

mediumLow.title: ReDoS / unbounded regex from unsanitized roleName params used in MongoDB $regex
mediumLow.description: POST /career-direction builds `new RegExp(degree, 'i')` directly from req.body.degree with NO escaping (line 554), unlike the other handlers which escape regex metacharacters. An attacker can send a catastrophic-backtracking pattern (e.g. '(a+)+$') or a broad '.*' to either DoS the query or match/enumerate unintended degree documents. /direction-roles escapes most metacharacters but the cleaned value is still used unanchored with $options:'i' across up to 10 OR'd fields, allowing broad enumeration. These endpoints have no auth (no protect) so the DoS is unauthenticated.
mediumLow.fix: Escape regex metacharacters on req.body.degree before constructing RegExp (reuse the existing escape pattern `s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')`), anchor the pattern, and cap input length. Consider exact-match or text-index lookups instead of unanchored case-insensitive regex. Apply auth where appropriate.

mediumLow.title: Unauthenticated retrieval of any user's saved analysis and PII via predictable trace IDs
mediumLow.description: GET /api/career-agent/dashboard/:id has no auth and returns the full stored analysis record including input_user_data (which contains personalDetails name/email, see onboarding save at lines 800-807). The id is a Date.now() timestamp (line 795) — guessable/enumerable — letting an unauthenticated attacker harvest other users' career analyses and PII from the records directory and Mongo (profile_hash fallback, line 1085). GET /user-skills/:email likewise returns any user's skill progress given only their email, with no auth and no ownership check.
mediumLow.fix: Require authentication on /dashboard/:id and /user-skills/:email and verify the requesting user owns the record (match req.user._id / req.user.email against the record). Stop using guessable Date.now() identifiers — use a random UUID or the Mongo ObjectId — and never return raw input_user_data PII to unauthorized callers.

mediumLow.title: Career analysis cache poisoning / cross-user data exposure via shared profile-hash file cache
mediumLow.description: makeProfileHash is computed only from education+preferences+skills (no user identity, lines 36-41). findCachedRecord scans the shared RECORDS_DIR and returns ANY user's stored analysis whose profile hash matches (lines 786-792), returning `analysis` from another user's record. Two different users with the same degree/skills/preferences will be served each other's cached output_generated_report, which can embed personalized/PII-influenced AI text. Combined with the unauthenticated /onboarding path, an attacker can also pre-seed the cache with a chosen profile to influence later identical-profile users.
mediumLow.fix: Include the authenticated userId in the profile hash, or scope the cache lookup to records owned by req.user. Store cache entries per-user rather than in a globally-scanned directory, and do not return another user's stored report.

mediumLow.title: CORS rejection errors propagate to the global error handler as 500s
mediumLow.description: callback(new Error('Not allowed by CORS')) creates a plain Error with no statusCode and isOperational falsy. It reaches errorHandler, which defaults statusCode to 500 and (in production) returns 'Something went very wrong!' with a 500. A blocked CORS origin is a client condition that should be 403, and logging it as a 500 server error pollutes error metrics/alerts and can mask real outages.
mediumLow.fix: Use new AppError('Not allowed by CORS', 403, 'CORS_BLOCKED') from utils/errors instead of a bare Error, so it is treated as an operational 403.

mediumLow.title: Morgan + logger.stream double-logs and an unbounded logs directory create write amplification / disk-fill risk
mediumLow.description: In production morgan('combined', { stream: logger.stream }) routes every HTTP line through logger.info, which writes to combined.log (5MB x 5 = 25MB cap, fine) but ALSO, because in production console.log is overridden to logger.info (server.js:18), any code path that console.logs goes through winston too. More importantly logger.stream.write calls logger.info on every request, doubling log volume and adding JSON-serialization overhead per request on the hot path. Combined with 50MB JSON body limit (line 99), large request logging amplifies memory/CPU.
mediumLow.fix: Keep morgan but write HTTP access logs to a dedicated rotating access.log transport rather than funneling through the general logger. Confirm log rotation caps (maxsize/maxFiles) are adequate for production traffic and consider winston-daily-rotate-file. Lower the 50MB body limit on routes that do not accept base64 images.

mediumLow.title: withRetry returns undefined instead of throwing on loop exhaustion
mediumLow.description: The while (attempt <= maxRetries) loop's throw on exhaustion is inside the catch and guarded by attempt > maxRetries, but the function can theoretically exit the loop and fall through to the implicit return undefined if the loop condition becomes false without a return/throw on a given path. Callers awaiting withRetry and expecting a value (or expecting a throw on failure) may instead receive undefined and proceed with bad data — silent corruption rather than an error. Also error.response.status comparison (status >= 400) when status is null evaluates null>=400 as false, which is the intended behavior, but relying on it is fragile.
mediumLow.fix: After the while loop add an explicit throw new Error('withRetry exhausted without returning'); to guarantee the function always either returns fn()'s value or throws. This makes the exhaustion contract explicit.

mediumLow.title: Every-minute todo-reminder cron has no overlap guard — concurrent runs can double-send notifications and pile up
mediumLow.description: The '* * * * *' job queries overdue todos and, per todo, creates a Notification then sets reminderTriggered=true and saves. If one run takes longer than 60s (DB slowness, large backlog), the next minute's run starts before the first marks reminderTriggered, so the same todos are fetched again and duplicate notifications are sent. There is no isRunning lock. Over time overlapping long runs also stack open DB operations.
mediumLow.fix: Add a module-level boolean lock: if (jobRunning) return; jobRunning = true; try { ... } finally { jobRunning = false; }. Better, mark reminderTriggered atomically: use Todo.updateMany or findOneAndUpdate with reminderTriggered:false in the filter so a row is claimed atomically before sending, eliminating the double-send window.

mediumLow.title: Analytics rollup builds college rankings with per-college sequential queries (N+1) — slow cron, connection pool pressure
mediumLow.description: For each active college the loop issues 3 sequential awaited DB operations (two countDocuments + one aggregate). With many colleges this is 3N round trips serialized, making the 3 AM rollup long-running and holding pool connections. runDailyRollup is also invoked at startup when no analytics exist (cronJobs.js:28-32) without awaiting, so a heavy rollup can run concurrently with server warm-up.
mediumLow.fix: Replace the per-college loop with a single aggregation pipeline that groups enrollments/students by college, or run the per-college work with bounded concurrency. Await or at least catch the startup rollup. This is performance hardening, not a correctness bug.

mediumLow.title: express.static serves the uploads directory twice, second mount exposes uploads at site root
mediumLow.description: Line 101 mounts uploads at /uploads (intended). Line 102 mounts the same uploads directory at the root path '/', so every uploaded file is also reachable directly at /<filename>. This widens the exposed surface, can shadow/conflict with API routes that share a top-level name, and serves user-uploaded content from the application origin root, increasing XSS/content-sniffing risk for user-supplied files.
mediumLow.fix: Remove line 102. Serve uploads only under the /uploads prefix. For user-uploaded content also set helmet/X-Content-Type-Options and consider serving from a separate domain or with Content-Disposition: attachment.

mediumLow.title: errorHandler clones the error with object spread, losing message/stack and non-enumerable AppError fields
mediumLow.description: let error = { ...err } spreads only own enumerable properties. On a native Error, message and stack are non-enumerable, so they are not copied; the code manually re-assigns error.message and error.name but NOT error.stack, and isOperational on AppError instances is reassigned via err.isOperational || false. The spread also discards the prototype, so instanceof AppError checks downstream fail. The result is error transformation that can mislabel an operational AppError as non-operational (leaking it into the generic 500 path) or vice-versa, and the production logger then logs an undefined stack.
mediumLow.fix: Do not shallow-spread errors. Operate on the original err (preserve prototype/stack) or use Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(err)) and copy properties including stack. Read isOperational directly from err. This ensures Mongoose/JWT transforms and the operational-vs-programming decision are reliable.

mediumLow.title: Coach.coachId unique without sparse allows null-collision on creation
mediumLow.description: coachId is declared `unique: true` but NOT `sparse: true`. coachId is assigned in a pre('save') hook; during the brief window before assignment (or if the hook errors), the value is null/undefined. With a non-sparse unique index, the second document with a null coachId throws a duplicate-key error. User/Student/Teacher correctly pair unique with sparse for their generated IDs.
