mediumLow.fix: Add `sparse: true` to the coachId field and declare the index explicitly: `coachId: { type: String, unique: true, sparse: true }` plus `coachSchema.index({ coachId: 1 }, { unique: true, sparse: true });`.

mediumLow.title: Course.courseCode unique without sparse and no required guard
mediumLow.description: courseCode is `unique: true` but not sparse; it is generated in pre-save. A failed/partial save with null courseCode collides with another null on the unique index. Additionally the explicit index at line 279 (`courseSchema.index({ courseCode: 1 })`) is a NON-unique duplicate of the inline unique declaration, which is redundant and can mask intent.
mediumLow.fix: Set `courseCode: { type: String, unique: true, sparse: true }` and remove the redundant non-unique `courseSchema.index({ courseCode: 1 })` at line 279 (the field-level unique already creates the index), or make that explicit index `{ unique: true, sparse: true }` and drop the inline option.

mediumLow.title: Assessment.assessmentCode unique without sparse
mediumLow.description: assessmentCode is `unique: true` but not sparse and is only populated in pre-save. As with Coach/Course, a null assessmentCode (pre-assignment or hook failure) collides under the non-sparse unique index causing duplicate-key errors on the second null.
mediumLow.fix: Change to `assessmentCode: { type: String, unique: true, sparse: true }`.

mediumLow.title: Duplicate handouts field definition in Course module schema
mediumLow.description: moduleSchema defines `handouts: [handoutSchema]` twice on consecutive lines (165 and 166). Mongoose silently uses the last definition and discards the first; while functionally harmless here (same definition), it indicates copy-paste error and will cause silent data issues if the two definitions ever diverge. It is a real schema defect.
mediumLow.fix: Delete the duplicate line 166 so `handouts: [handoutSchema]` is declared only once.

mediumLow.title: Enrollment.calculateProgress counts modules but Course progress logic counts days — inconsistent and uses .save() inside method
mediumLow.description: Enrollment.calculateProgress computes progress as completedModules/totalModules, while the parallel CourseEnrollment model computes progress by completed days. The two enrollment models (Enrollment and CourseEnrollment) model the same domain with divergent progress semantics and both reference different student collections (Enrollment.student -> 'Student', CourseEnrollment.student -> 'User'), creating referential-integrity ambiguity about which collection a student actually lives in. Additionally calculateProgress calls this.save() internally, so callers that also save will double-write and can trigger parallel-save errors.
mediumLow.fix: Decide on a single source of truth for enrollment/progress; if both must coexist, document and align the student ref (both should point to the same canonical model). Remove the internal `await this.save()` from calculateProgress and have callers persist explicitly, or rename it to clarify it persists.

mediumLow.title: User.assignedTeacher references 'User' while Student.assignedTeacher references 'Teacher' — referential inconsistency
mediumLow.description: In User.js, assignedTeacher ref is 'User'; in Student.js the same logical field refs 'Teacher'. Since teachers exist both as User documents (role 'teacher') and as Teacher documents, populate() on assignedTeacher resolves to different collections depending on which model holds the student. This breaks populate joins and produces null/incorrect teacher data depending on code path.
mediumLow.fix: Standardize the teacher entity. Pick one collection (Teacher or User-with-role) as canonical and make both assignedTeacher refs point to it. Migrate existing ObjectIds accordingly.

mediumLow.title: Course embedded question correctAnswer type mismatch: Number vs String
mediumLow.description: Within Course, daySchema.videoContent.embeddedQuestions.correctAnswer (line 101) and daySchema.tasks.correctAnswer (line 111) are typed `Number`, while the reusable quizSchema.correctAnswer (line 6) and Assessment/QuestionBank correctAnswer are `String`/Mixed. The same conceptual data (the correct option) is stored as a numeric index in some embedded paths and a string elsewhere. Grading/comparison code comparing these across paths will mismatch types (e.g. 1 !== '1'), producing wrong scoring.
mediumLow.fix: Pick one representation for correctAnswer across all question shapes (recommend Mixed or String consistently) and align daySchema.tasks.correctAnswer and embeddedQuestions.correctAnswer to match quizSchema. Update grading code to normalize types before comparison.

mediumLow.title: Missing index on Result.assessmentId and CourseEnrollment student/course lookups for common access patterns
mediumLow.description: Result indexes cover {userId,assessmentId} and {userId,completionStatus} and {submittedAt}, but there is no standalone index on assessmentId for queries that aggregate all results of an assessment (analytics/averageScore computations) which scan the full collection. As result volume grows these become slow.
mediumLow.fix: Add `resultSchema.index({ assessmentId: 1, completionStatus: 1 });` to support per-assessment analytics queries.

mediumLow.title: Assessment.duration marked required but has a default — validation is effectively dead
mediumLow.description: duration is both `required: true` and `default: 1440`. Because the default always supplies a value, the required validator can never fail, so the constraint is misleading/dead. If the intent was to force callers to set a duration, the default defeats it.
mediumLow.fix: Decide intent: either remove `default` to genuinely enforce required, or remove `required: true` since a default is always present. Keep only one.

mediumLow.title: Student.mustChangePassword and isFirstLogin default true may conflict with non-onboarded creation paths
mediumLow.description: mustChangePassword defaults true and isFirstLogin defaults true. Any student created through an admin/import path that sets a final password will still be flagged to change password and treated as first login, forcing an unintended password-reset flow. This is a default-value bug for non-self-registration creation paths.
mediumLow.fix: Make these defaults explicit at creation sites (set false for admin-created/imported students) or default them to false and set true only in the self-registration flow. Confirm the intended onboarding behavior with the auth flow.

mediumLow.title: Coach model stores credentials/contact but has no password/select:false and email lacks validation
mediumLow.description: Coach.email is unique+lowercase but lacks the email-format `match` validator used by User/Student/Teacher, and mobile lacks the 10-digit validator. Inconsistent validation lets malformed coach contact data into the DB.
mediumLow.fix: Add the same `match: [/^\w+([.-]?\w+)*@\w+([.-]?\w+)*(\.\w{2,3})+$/, 'Please provide a valid email']` to email and the 10-digit regex validator to mobile, matching the other identity models.

mediumLow.title: Notification 30-day TTL index deletes unread/important notifications
mediumLow.description: `notificationSchema.index({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 30*24*60*60 })` unconditionally deletes every notification 30 days after creation, regardless of read state or type. Unread notifications (including 'certificate', 'suspension', 'warning', 'support') silently vanish after 30 days even if the user never saw them. Users can lose record of warnings/suspensions and certificate issuance.
mediumLow.fix: Either remove the TTL and prune via a scheduled job that only deletes READ, low-priority notifications, or implement a partial TTL keyed off a separate `expiresAt` field set only for ephemeral types. MongoDB TTL cannot be conditional on `isRead`, so the robust approach is a per-document `expiresAt: Date` field (null for must-keep types) with `index({ expiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 })`.

mediumLow.title: Certificate.recordVerification uses non-atomic read-modify-write (lost increments)
mediumLow.description: `recordVerification` does `this.verificationCount += 1; this.lastVerifiedAt = new Date(); return this.save();`. This is a read-modify-write on the in-memory document. Concurrent verifications of the same public certificate (a verify endpoint is inherently exposed to parallel hits) read the same base count and overwrite each other, undercounting verifications. The full document save also risks clobbering other concurrent field updates.
mediumLow.fix: Replace with an atomic update: `return this.constructor.findByIdAndUpdate(this._id, { $inc: { verificationCount: 1 }, $set: { lastVerifiedAt: new Date() } }, { new: true });` so the increment is performed server-side.

mediumLow.title: UserCertificate.qrCodeIdentifier uses only 24 bits of randomness with no collision retry
mediumLow.description: `qrCodeIdentifier` is `unique: true` but generated as `EXT-${year}-${crypto.randomBytes(3).toString('hex')}` — only 3 random bytes (16.7M values) scoped per year. By the birthday bound, collisions become likely within tens of thousands of certs per year, and the pre-save hook has no detect-and-retry loop. On collision the save throws an unhandled E11000 and certificate creation fails. The `unique` index also has no `sparse`/partial filter, so any legacy docs with null qrCodeIdentifier would collide on null.
mediumLow.fix: Increase entropy (e.g. `crypto.randomBytes(8)`), and wrap save/generation in a retry loop that regenerates on E11000. Add `{ unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { qrCodeIdentifier: { $type: 'string' } } }` (or sparse) to tolerate nulls. Same hardening should be applied to Certificate.certificateId generation.

mediumLow.title: Notification denormalized userId/recipient and isRead/read can drift outside createNotification
mediumLow.description: The schema duplicates two pairs of fields: userId/recipient and isRead/read. Only the static `createNotification` syncs them; any code path that constructs `new Notification(...)` directly, or marks a single notification read via `findByIdAndUpdate({ isRead: true })` without also setting `read`, leaves the two flags inconsistent. Because `getUnreadCount`/`markAllAsRead` query an `$or` over BOTH fields (lines 149-167), a notification marked read on only one flag still counts as unread, so the badge count never clears — a visible UX bug.
mediumLow.fix: Collapse to a single source of truth. Pick one canonical field (e.g. `recipient` + `isRead`), migrate data, and remove the duplicate. If both must remain for compatibility, add a pre-save hook that mirrors the pair on every save AND a pre-findOneAndUpdate/pre-updateMany hook that mirrors `$set` of either flag to the other, so no write path can desync them.

mediumLow.title: VisionBoardPro userId typed as Mixed defeats the userId index and ownership queries
mediumLow.description: `userId` is `mongoose.Schema.Types.Mixed` 'to handle both String and ObjectId without forced casting'. The model also declares `index({ userId: 1, createdAt: -1 })`. With Mixed type, the same user can be stored sometimes as an ObjectId and sometimes as a string, so an ownership query `find({ userId: someObjectId })` will NOT match documents where it was saved as a string (and vice-versa). This silently hides a user's own boards and is an authorization hazard (a board could be fetched/missed inconsistently).
mediumLow.fix: Normalize to a single type. Change to `type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'User'` and cast at the controller boundary, OR add a pre-save/normalization step that always stores the canonical form. Run a migration to convert existing string userIds to ObjectId so the index and queries are consistent.

mediumLow.title: UserBadge progress percentage can exceed 100 and earned state is never reset
mediumLow.description: The pre-save computes `percentage = round(current/target*100)` and auto-sets `isEarned` once >=100, but never clamps to 100 and never reverts isEarned if progress later drops (e.g. a streak badge whose streak resets). Stored percentages above 100 leak into the UI, and a badge once auto-earned stays earned even if the underlying criterion is no longer met, causing denormalization drift against the real metric.
mediumLow.fix: Clamp: `this.progress.percentage = Math.min(100, Math.round((current/target)*100))`. Decide explicit semantics for revocation: if badges are permanent, document that and ignore decreases; if they should reflect current state (streaks), recompute isEarned from percentage rather than only latching it true.

mediumLow.title: Note unique index on (user, courseId) will throw on concurrent first-note creation
mediumLow.description: `noteSchema.index({ user: 1, courseId: 1 }, { unique: true })` enforces one note per user/course. Any create-if-missing flow that does findOne-then-create (rather than upsert) will throw an unhandled E11000 when the same user saves a note for a course twice in quick succession (double save / autosave), surfacing a 500 to the user.
mediumLow.fix: Persist notes via `findOneAndUpdate({ user, courseId }, { $set: { title, content, lastUpdated: Date.now() } }, { upsert: true, new: true, setDefaultsOnInsert: true })` so the unique constraint is satisfied atomically, and handle E11000 as a no-op merge.

mediumLow.title: Final question shuffle seeds with Date.now(), breaking the documented deterministic ordering
mediumLow.description: shuffleArrayDeterministic is documented (and used throughout selection) so the 'Same user ID will always get the same shuffled order'. But the final return seeds with `${userId}_${stageKey}_final_${Date.now()}_${length}`. Because Date.now() changes every call, the final order is NOT deterministic: if the assessment is regenerated (page reload, retry, server re-fetch of the same attempt), the question order changes. Any code that stored answers by position/index, or that expects the same order on re-fetch within one attempt, will mismatch answers to questions. The selected set is stable but the presentation order is not.
mediumLow.fix: Seed the final shuffle with a stable per-attempt key, not Date.now(). Pass an explicit attemptId/attemptNumber into selectStratifiedQuestionsForStage and use `${userId}_${stageKey}_final_${attemptId}`. If different ordering per attempt is genuinely desired, the order must be persisted with the attempt so re-fetches reproduce it, rather than being recomputed from wall-clock time.

mediumLow.title: Pass-1 quotient-wide fallback index is shared and consumed across difficulty buckets, can starve later buckets
mediumLow.description: `fallbackIndex` and `shuffledQuotientPool` are built once per quotient, then advanced monotonically (fallbackIndex++) across each difficulty bucket's shortfall loop. Earlier buckets that pull from the shared pool advance the index past questions that later buckets could have used, and the loop only checks `selectedIds.has` to skip already-picked. If an early difficulty bucket consumes a large slice, a later bucket within the same quotient can hit the end of shuffledQuotientPool (fallbackIndex >= length) and remain short even though unselected questions for that quotient still exist earlier in the pool that were skipped only because they were iterated past. This yields fewer questions than the stage distribution requires.
mediumLow.fix: Reset/rescan the quotient-wide pool per difficulty bucket, or iterate the whole shuffledQuotientPool each time (for...of with a selectedIds guard) instead of carrying a monotonic fallbackIndex. The global Pass-2 fallback partly masks this but pulls cross-quotient, violating the per-quotient distribution intent.

mediumLow.title: Streak 6-day milestone keyed to exact equality can be skipped by grace-period jumps
mediumLow.description: The grace-period branch increments currentStreak by exactly 1 even after missing 1-2 active days, so the streak value still passes through every integer and `=== 6` will normally be hit. However, the milestone award is gated on `streak.currentStreak === 6` exactly. Combined with restoreStreak (line 235) which sets currentStreak directly to preResetStreak (e.g. jumping from 1 to 9), a restored user who was already past 6 never re-triggers, and any future logic that adjusts streak by more than 1 would skip the milestone entirely. The exact-equality milestone check is fragile.
mediumLow.fix: Award the milestone when crossing the threshold rather than landing exactly on it: check `streak.currentStreak >= 6` combined with the existing idempotency guard (UserAchievement of type STREAK_6_DAYS not already present). The existing milestoneExists query already prevents duplicates, so >= is safe and robust to jumps.

mediumLow.title: restoreStreak matches any active voucher, not the streak-restoration voucher type
mediumLow.description: restoreStreak finds an achievement by `{ user, 'voucher.code', 'voucher.status':'Active' }` with no constraint on achievementType. Any active voucher the user holds for any achievement (current or future achievement types that include a voucher subdocument) can be redeemed to restore a streak, and it is consumed (status set to Redeemed) even if it was intended for a different benefit. This lets unrelated vouchers be burned for streak restoration.
mediumLow.fix: Scope the lookup to the streak voucher type, e.g. add `achievementType: 'STREAK_6_DAYS'` (or a dedicated voucherType: 'STREAK_RESTORE' field) to the findOne query so only restoration vouchers are accepted and consumed.

mediumLow.title: Assessment results email mislabels score-only assessments as 'Needs Improvement'
mediumLow.description: When maxScore is falsy, percentage is set to null. performanceLabel/performanceColor are then computed from `percentage >= 80 ? ... : ... : 'Needs Improvement'`. `null >= 80` (and all the others) is false, so every score-only assessment (no maxScore) is always labeled 'Needs Improvement' in red, regardless of the actual score, which is shown raw in the circle. This sends an alarming/incorrect performance label to students.
mediumLow.fix: Guard the label computation on percentage !== null. When percentage is null (no maxScore), omit the performanceLabel/performanceColor entirely or pick a neutral label/color, e.g. `const performanceLabel = percentage === null ? '' : (percentage >= 80 ? 'Excellent' : ...)` and only render the label block when a percentage exists.

mediumLow.title: updateTaskProgress blindly replaces entire completedTasks object (data loss + unbounded write)
mediumLow.description: updateTaskProgress accepts any client-supplied object for completedTasks and does `$set: { completedTasks }`, fully overwriting the stored map. A client that sends a partial or stale object silently erases previously completed tasks (e.g. two tabs/devices racing, or a client that only sends the delta). There is also no shape/size validation beyond typeof object, so arbitrary nested data can be persisted.
mediumLow.fix: Either merge keys instead of replacing (read existing, merge truthy completions, then save; or use dotted $set per task key like `$set: { ['completedTasks.'+taskId]: true }`), and validate that values are the expected primitive (boolean/known shape). If full replacement is intended, document it and have the client always send the complete authoritative map; otherwise switch to per-task updates to avoid clobbering.

mediumLow.title: resolveUserEmail returns null on any DB error, indistinguishable from 'user not found'
mediumLow.description: resolveUserEmail wraps the Student/User lookup in try/catch and returns null on any thrown error (connection failure, cast error, etc.), identical to the legitimate not-found result. Callers that decide whether to send an email cannot distinguish a transient DB failure from a genuinely missing user, so emails are silently dropped during outages with no logging.
mediumLow.fix: Log the caught error (console.error) before returning null, and consider distinguishing not-found (return null) from infrastructure errors (rethrow or return a sentinel) so callers can retry transient failures instead of silently skipping notifications.

mediumLow.title: College leaderboard groups enrollments by ObjectId used as object key, relying on implicit toString
mediumLow.description: studentStats is keyed with `studentStats[s._id]` where s._id is a Mongoose ObjectId; lookups later use `studentStats[e.student._id]`. Object property keys are coerced via toString(), which happens to work for ObjectId, but it is fragile: if e.student is ever an unpopulated ObjectId vs a populated doc, or if populate fails (e.student null), `e.student._id` throws. Line 261 also does `studentStats[sId].totalTime += e.totalTimeSpent` with no `|| 0` guard, so a missing totalTimeSpent yields NaN that propagates into totalHours.
mediumLow.fix: Normalize keys explicitly with String(s._id) / String(e.student?._id), guard against e.student being null after populate, and default numeric fields: `studentStats[sId].totalTime += (e.totalTimeSpent || 0)` and `+= (e.progress || 0)` to prevent NaN in the leaderboard.

mediumLow.title: Signup tempToken stored in sessionStorage and used as the OTP auth credential
mediumLow.description: The signup OTP flow stores `data.tempToken` in sessionStorage and later submits it to /auth/verify-signup-otp and /auth/resend-signup-otp as the sole credential binding the OTP to the user. sessionStorage is readable by any JS in the page, so any XSS (e.g. via the many unsanitized user-rendered fields elsewhere) can steal the tempToken and complete or hijack the signup verification. It is a bearer-style secret kept in JS-accessible storage.
mediumLow.fix: Have the backend set the signup tempToken as an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie (the app already uses `credentials: 'include'`), and verify the OTP against that cookie rather than a value echoed back through client storage. If a client value must be kept, scope it to in-memory React state for the single-page flow rather than sessionStorage.

mediumLow.title: Stale API_BASE_URL used by Profile/Settings raw fetches bypasses fallback-port discovery
mediumLow.description: `API_BASE_URL` is computed once at module load (api.js:15) and exported with `export let`. The real request logic in apiCall uses a discovered `workingBaseUrl` (probing ports 5001/5002 on failure) but never reassigns the exported `API_BASE_URL`. Profile.jsx and Settings.jsx build URLs directly from the imported `API_BASE_URL`, so when the backend is not on the default port these pages hit the wrong port and all their saves/uploads fail even though the rest of the app (via apiCall) works. The mismatch is invisible to the user beyond a generic error toast.
mediumLow.fix: Use `apiCall` for these requests so they share the discovered base URL, or export and consume `getBackendUrl()`/the resolved `workingBaseUrl` rather than the frozen `API_BASE_URL` snapshot.

mediumLow.title: OTP auto-submit race: 6th digit triggers submit before React state commits
mediumLow.description: On reaching 6 digits the onChange schedules `document.getElementById('otp-submit-btn').click()` after 100ms. The submit handler reads `otp` from React state. Because the click is fired via a detached setTimeout and the handler closes over state, fast typing or paste plus a re-render can cause the click to occur with a stale `otp` (e.g. 5 digits) or fire twice (once via auto-click, once if the user also presses Enter). The 100ms guess is timing-dependent and not reliable; double-submission can consume/burn the OTP attempt count on the backend and lock the user out faster.
mediumLow.fix: Drive auto-submit from a useEffect keyed on `otp` length (`useEffect(() => { if (otp.length === 6 && timeLeft > 0) handleVerifyOTP(); }, [otp])`) so it runs after state commit, and add an `isLoading`/submitted guard at the top of handleVerifyOTP to prevent duplicate submissions. Avoid synthetic DOM clicks.

mediumLow.title: ComprehensiveSignup writes registration flags into sessionStorage but never validates otpVerified
mediumLow.description: VerifyOTP sets `sessionStorage.setItem('otpVerified','true')` then navigates to /signup. ComprehensiveSignup's mount guard (lines 34-46) only checks for the presence of `signupEmail`/`user` and `hasRegistration`; it never checks `otpVerified`. A user (or anyone) can navigate directly to /signup with just a `signupEmail` set (e.g. from a partial SignupInitial run that failed OTP) and reach the full registration form, submitting register-details without ever verifying the OTP. The client-side gate intended by the OTP step is not enforced.
mediumLow.fix: In ComprehensiveSignup's mount effect, redirect to /verify-otp (or /signup-initial) when `sessionStorage.getItem('otpVerified') !== 'true'` for new (non-logged-in) signups. Ensure the backend also rejects register-details for unverified emails as the authoritative check.

mediumLow.title: ComprehensiveSignup success path assumes sessionStorage 'user' exists, can throw and abort redirect
mediumLow.description: After a successful register-details POST, the code reads `sessionStorage.getItem('user')` and `JSON.parse`s it to set hasRegistration. In the signup flow the user typically arrives with only `signupEmail`/`signupFullName` set and no `user` object (login happens after signup). When `user` is absent the flag update is skipped, but if `user` exists and is malformed the unguarded JSON.parse throws inside the try block AFTER setIsSuccess(true) but the throw jumps to catch which calls setIsLoading(false) and a toast, leaving the success screen rendered with no redirect (the setTimeout navigate never registers). The user is stuck on 'Profile 100% Completed' forever.
mediumLow.fix: Wrap the JSON.parse in its own try/catch, and move the `setTimeout(navigate...)` so it is scheduled before/independent of the sessionStorage update so a parse failure cannot prevent the redirect.

mediumLow.title: DOB age validation is incorrect — month-only check lets under-16 users through
mediumLow.description: Age is computed as `today.getFullYear() - dobDate.getFullYear()` and only rejected when `age < 16 || (age === 16 && m < 0)` where m is the month difference. This ignores the day-of-month and mis-handles the boundary: someone who turns 16 later this month (age===16, m===0 but birthday not yet reached) passes, and the `age<16` branch already covers the m check making the second clause inconsistent. Year-of-passing must-be-greater-than year-of-study (line 185) also wrongly forbids students whose study year equals passing year.
mediumLow.fix: Compute age properly: `let age = today.getFullYear()-dob.getFullYear(); const md = today.getMonth()-dob.getMonth(); if (md < 0 || (md===0 && today.getDate()<dob.getDate())) age--; if (age < 16) reject;`. Re-evaluate the yearOfPassing>=yearOfStudy rule (use >= rather than >).

mediumLow.title: register-section saves are fire-and-forget with silent failure, causing perceived data loss
mediumLow.description: saveSection() swallows all errors ('Silent fail - don't block the user') and handleNextStep awaits it but ignores the result. If the progressive save 401s (e.g. token expired) or the network is down, the user advances through all 11 steps believing data is saved; only the final submit reveals failure (or also silently loses the per-step data). Combined with the missing-auth-header issues, partial registrations can be silently dropped.
mediumLow.fix: Surface non-network save failures with a non-blocking warning toast and a retry, or at minimum detect 401 and route through apiCall so the standard session-expiry redirect fires. Persist a 'dirty/unsaved' indicator so the user knows a step did not save.

mediumLow.title: AddDetails has no per-step validation and submits future/invalid dates
mediumLow.description: Unlike ComprehensiveSignup, AddDetails' handleNextStep performs zero validation and handleSubmit performs none either. Work-experience start/end dates, percentages, required fields, and URL formats are all accepted as-is. A user can submit an end date before the start date, a percentage of 999, or empty required fields, and the only feedback is whatever the backend returns. Inconsistent with the stricter create-flow, leading to corrupt profile data.
mediumLow.fix: Extract the validation functions from ComprehensiveSignup into a shared module and reuse them in AddDetails handleNextStep/handleSubmit, including date-order and percentage-range checks.

mediumLow.title: AddDetails profile-photo upload reads e.target.files[0] without null guard and uses res.url unchecked
mediumLow.description: The inline file onChange does `const file = e.target.files[0]` then uploads; on a successful apiCall it does `setPersonalDetails({...personalDetails, profilePhoto: res.url})` without checking that res or res.url exists. If the /upload response shape differs (e.g. {data:{url}} or an error object that still resolves), profilePhoto is set to undefined and the avatar silently breaks. The catch only toasts a generic 'Upload failed'.
mediumLow.fix: Validate the response: `if (res?.url) setPersonalDetails(...); else toast.error('Upload failed')`. Also reset `e.target.value` after upload so re-selecting the same file re-triggers onChange.

mediumLow.title: LockedOut 'Appeal Lockout' and 'Go to Dashboard' may loop a still-locked user
mediumLow.description: Both actions link into /dashboard routes. A user who was locked out of an assessment is sent to /dashboard, but there is no state cleared or flag passed indicating the lockout was acknowledged. If the dashboard or a guard re-checks the disqualified attempt and bounces them back to the assessment (which then re-triggers the lockout), the user can be stuck in a redirect loop. The reason is also taken purely from location.state with a generic fallback, so a direct visit to /locked-out shows a scary 'Disqualified' message with no context.
mediumLow.fix: Confirm the dashboard route does not re-route a disqualified user back into the assessment; consider clearing the in-progress assessment/timer storage on this page mount. For direct/stateless visits, show a softer neutral message rather than a hard disqualification claim.

mediumLow.title: MicroAssessmentPlayer score NaN when totalPoints is 0
mediumLow.description: handleSubmit computes pct: Math.round((score / totalPoints) * 100). totalPoints is summed from q.points||1 over activeQuestions, so if the assessment has zero questions (empty assessmentData.questions) totalPoints is 0 and pct becomes NaN. The result screen then renders 'NaN%' in ScoreRing and the strokeDashoffset math produces NaN, breaking the SVG ring. An assessment can reach 'taking' with 0 questions because handleStart/maxTime guard with Math.max(totalQ,1) but submission math does not.
mediumLow.fix: Guard the division: const pct = totalPoints > 0 ? Math.round((score/totalPoints)*100) : 0. Also early-return or show an empty-state if activeQuestions.length === 0 before allowing the quiz to start.

mediumLow.title: BaseLineTest answer persistence index restore can land on already-answered question / off-by-one
mediumLow.description: On resume, firstUnansweredIndex is computed against sortedQuestions (the full fetched list), but the active questions array is limitedQuestions = sortedQuestions.slice(0, questionLimit) (line 449). If a previously-answered question lies beyond questionLimit, or counts differ, the restored index can point outside the rendered set or to an inconsistent position. Also, when all are answered it sets index to sortedQuestions.length-1 which may exceed limitedQuestions.length-1, leaving 'current' undefined and rendering a blank question with no options.
mediumLow.fix: Compute the resume index against limitedQuestions, not sortedQuestions, and clamp: setIndex(Math.min(firstUnansweredIndex===-1?limitedQuestions.length-1:firstUnansweredIndex, limitedQuestions.length-1)). Use limitedQuestions consistently for the all-answered branch.

mediumLow.title: BaseLineTest timer effect depends on submit, recreating interval and losing one-minute-alert guard semantics
mediumLow.description: The countdown useEffect lists submit in its dependency array (line 675). submit is a useCallback whose deps include selectedAnswers-derived allQuestionsAnswered and other frequently-changing values, so submit is re-created often. Each recreation tears down and recreates the 1s interval. While timerStartRef persists the real start time (so remaining time is correct), the repeated teardown/setup is wasteful and, combined with reading oneMinuteAlertShownRef only at setup, can cause the one-minute alert to fire inconsistently or the interval to briefly stop around answer changes. The timeoutSubmitTriggeredRef guard mitigates double-submit but the churn is fragile.
mediumLow.fix: Stabilize submit (memoize allQuestionsAnswered separately and keep submit deps minimal, or read latest values via refs) and remove submit from the interval effect deps, invoking the latest submit through a ref. The interval should be created once per (loading,resultId,submitted) transition.

mediumLow.title: QuotientsGrid flashes 'No Assessment Data Found' empty state during load
mediumLow.description: The render branches on !baselineData to show the empty 'No Assessment Data Found / Take Assessment' panel, but loading is never consulted in the JSX. While the fetch is in flight, baselineData is null so users who actually completed the baseline briefly see the 'you have not completed the assessment' CTA before their quotient cards pop in — a confusing flash and a potential mis-click to retake.
mediumLow.fix: Add a loading guard before the empty state, e.g. render a skeleton/spinner when loading is true, and only show the empty state when !loading && !baselineData.

mediumLow.title: ModuleViewPage route guard permanently disabled via if(false), dead unlock logic
mediumLow.description: The sequential-progression route guard effect computes isActuallyUnlocked and isModuleAllowed but then gates the enforcement behind `if (false)` (line 325), so the guard never runs and isDayUnlocked always returns true (line 626). This means locking/gating advertised to users ('Finish previous session to unlock') is not enforced at all, and the computed values plus the effect's large dependency array run on every change for no effect. If sequential gating is a product requirement this is a functional gap; if not, it is dead code that should be removed.
mediumLow.fix: Decide intent: either enable the guard (replace if(false) with if(!isActuallyUnlocked || !isModuleAllowed)) and make isDayUnlocked actually evaluate completion, or delete the disabled guard block and the unused isModuleAllowed/isActuallyUnlocked computations to remove confusion and wasted renders.

mediumLow.title: ModuleTasks renders unstyled 'Module not found' and task toggle is a no-op
mediumLow.description:
ModuleTasks is built entirely on hardcoded mock data (lines 15-23). For any moduleId not in 1-4 it renders a bare '
Module not found
' with no styling, header, or back navigation — a dead end. Additionally handleTaskToggle only console.logs (line 72-75), so checkboxes never change state and the progress bar/Next Module button can never reflect real progress. If this page is reachable in production it presents fake, non-functional data to users.
mediumLow.fix: Either wire this page to the real course/enrollment API (like ModuleViewPage) or remove the route if superseded. At minimum render a styled not-found state with a back-to-courses action, and make handleTaskToggle update local state so the UI is consistent.

mediumLow.title: GroupChat message sequential-grouping indexes wrong array when search is active
mediumLow.description: Inside the render of filteredMessages, isSequential is computed as `idx > 0 && group.messages[idx - 1].sender === msg.sender`. But `idx` is the index into the FILTERED array (filteredMessages), while it indexes into the UNFILTERED `group.messages`. When a message search filter is active (msgSearchQuery), or any messages are filtered, idx no longer aligns with group.messages, so the 'is this message from the same sender as the previous one' check compares against the wrong message. This causes sender-name labels to incorrectly appear/disappear above messages during search.
mediumLow.fix: Compute sequential grouping against the same array being mapped: `const isSequential = idx > 0 && filteredMessages[idx - 1].sender === msg.sender;`. The filteredMessages array is already in scope inside the IIFE.

mediumLow.title: GroupChat uses array index as React key for messages
mediumLow.description: Messages are rendered with `key={idx}` (the filtered-array index) instead of `msg._id`. Because the list is re-fetched every 3 seconds (polling) and is also filtered by search, indices shift when messages are added/removed or the filter changes. React then reuses DOM/component state across different logical messages, which can cause the wrong message to receive the long-press emoji picker, reaction state, the pin highlight ring, or animation state — and can drop/duplicate the smooth-scroll and ring-highlight applied to id=`msg-${msg._id}`. Each message already has a stable _id (used in id=`msg-${msg._id}`).
mediumLow.fix: Use the stable id as the key: `key={msg._id}`. Keep the array index only for non-identity concerns. This makes reaction pickers, pin highlights, and scroll-to-message target the correct element after each 3s poll refresh.

mediumLow.title: GroupChat 3-second polling has no overlap guard / no abort on unmount race
mediumLow.description: fetchGroupDetails is polled via setInterval every 3000ms (line 84) and is also called manually after send/vote/react/pin. There is no in-flight guard: if a request takes longer than 3s (slow network / large group object with embedded base64 media) requests stack up, and responses can arrive out of order so an older group snapshot can overwrite a newer one (setGroup(res.data) with stale data), causing messages/reactions/poll votes to visibly flicker or revert. Since whole group (including base64 image/video data URLs stored inline) is re-fetched every 3s, this is also heavy bandwidth/CPU. The interval is cleared on unmount but an in-flight promise can still call setGroup after unmount.
mediumLow.fix: Guard against overlap and staleness: keep a `isFetching` ref and skip the poll if a request is already in flight; or use an AbortController and abort the previous request before starting a new one; track a monotonically increasing request id and ignore responses that are not the latest. Also set a mounted ref (or use AbortController) so setGroup is not called after unmount. Consider a dedicated messages endpoint with since-timestamp paging instead of refetching the entire group (with inline media) every 3s.

mediumLow.title: GroupChat send button disabled state ignores polls (cannot send poll-only message via send button)
mediumLow.description: The submit button is disabled when `(!messageInput.trim() && !selectedMedia)`. handleSendMessage, however, also allows sending when a valid poll exists (pollToSend). So a user who opens the poll editor and fills a valid poll but types no text and attaches no media sees the main form's send button greyed out; the form's onSubmit path cannot fire. (The modal's own 'Send Poll' button works, but the disabled main button is inconsistent and confusing.)
mediumLow.fix: Include poll validity in the disabled expression, e.g. compute `const hasValidPoll = showPollEditor && pollData.question.trim() && pollData.options.filter(o=>o.trim()).length>=2;` and use `disabled={sending || (!messageInput.trim() && !selectedMedia && !hasValidPoll)}`. This keeps the disabled state in sync with what handleSendMessage actually accepts.

mediumLow.title: GroupChat searchStudents/addMember compare student ids against populated member objects
mediumLow.description: handleSearchStudents filters results with `!group.members.includes(s._id)`. Elsewhere the component treats members as populated objects (group.memberDetails with member._id, and group.admins as objects via a._id||a). If group.members is an array of populated member objects (or of ObjectId-like values) rather than plain string ids, `.includes(s._id)` (string compare by reference/value) will not match, so already-existing members are not filtered out of the add-member search and can be 're-added' (server may reject, surfacing the misleading 'different university' alert at line 252).
mediumLow.fix: Normalize ids before comparing: build a Set of member id strings, e.g. `const memberIds = new Set((group.members||[]).map(m => (m._id||m).toString())); const validResults = res.data.filter(s => !memberIds.has(s._id.toString()));`. Apply the same id-normalization pattern already used for admins (a._id||a).toString().

mediumLow.title: GroupChat renders user-supplied senderName/content via mention parser but message text is otherwise safe; shared/image URLs rendered into src without scheme validation
mediumLow.description: No dangerouslySetInnerHTML is used (good — renderMessageContent builds React nodes, so message text is auto-escaped). However img/video src and the in-app media viewer use raw user-controlled URLs: msg.image, msg.video, msg.sharedPost.media.url are placed directly into src. Because uploads go through FileReader as data: URLs this is usually fine, but sharedPost.media.url and any server-stored URL are not scheme-validated, allowing `javascript:`-style or untrusted external URLs to be loaded; an attacker-controlled media URL could be used for tracking/SSRF-style fetches or to load unexpected content. Lower severity since src on img/video does not execute JS, but it is unvalidated user content rendered to the DOM.
mediumLow.fix: Before using any message media URL in src, validate the scheme: allow only `https:`, `http:`, and `data:image/`,`data:video/` prefixes; reject anything else (render a placeholder). Centralize in a helper `safeMediaUrl(url)` and use it for msg.image, msg.video, viewerMedia.url, and msg.sharedPost.media.url. This prevents loading attacker-chosen schemes/hosts.

mediumLow.title: StudentGroups create-modal useEffect missing location dependency; create-intent only honored on first mount
mediumLow.description: The mount effect reads location.state?.create to auto-open the create modal, but the dependency array is empty ([]). If the user is already on /dashboard/groups and navigates again with state {create:true} (e.g. from a 'Create Group' shortcut elsewhere), the effect does not re-run, so the modal does not open. Also window.history.replaceState({}, ...) mutates history outside React Router, which can desync router state (location.state remains in React Router's in-memory state on back/forward), so the modal could unexpectedly reopen on navigation in some flows.
mediumLow.fix: Add location.state (or location.key) to the dependency array and gate on it: `useEffect(()=>{ if (location.state?.create) { setShowCreateModal(true); navigate(location.pathname, { replace: true, state: {} }); } }, [location]);`. Use react-router's navigate(..., {replace:true, state:{}}) to clear the intent instead of window.history.replaceState so router state stays consistent.

mediumLow.title: Resume preview crashes if saved/synced skills field is an array instead of a comma-string
mediumLow.description: The render does `resumeData.skills.technical.split(',')` (and the same for .soft line 1711 and .languages line 1727), guarded only by truthiness `{resumeData.skills.technical && (...)}`. resumeData.skills comes from two sources: (a) a saved resume from the DB at line 418 `skills: r.skills || {technical:'',soft:'',languages:''}` — `r.skills` is taken verbatim from the backend, so if the stored document ever has `technical` as an array (a very plausible shape given skills are arrays elsewhere, e.g. profile `data.skills` is an array joined at line 499) the truthiness guard passes and `.split` throws `TypeError: .split is not a function`, white-screening the entire resume builder; (b) even an object missing the field is fine, but any non-string truthy value crashes. There is no normalization of r.skills on load.
mediumLow.fix: Normalize skills on load and harden the render. On load (line 418) coerce each subfield: `skills: { technical: Array.isArray(r.skills?.technical) ? r.skills.technical.join(', ') : (r.skills?.technical || ''), soft: ..., languages: ... }`. Defensively, in the render replace `resumeData.skills.technical.split(',')` with `String(resumeData.skills.technical || '').split(',')` for all three fields so a malformed value degrades gracefully instead of crashing.

mediumLow.title: Unguarded JSON.parse of sessionStorage 'userData' can white-screen ProfileAnalysis
mediumLow.description: In the mount effect, `const userDataStr = sessionStorage.getItem('userData'); if (userDataStr) { setUserData(JSON.parse(userDataStr)); }`. JSON.parse is not wrapped in try/catch. If sessionStorage 'userData' is corrupted or holds the literal string 'undefined' (a common artifact of `sessionStorage.setItem('userData', String(value))`), JSON.parse throws synchronously inside the effect and the component fails to render. Other files in this audit (VisionBoardEditorPro getDraftKey, CareerAgentDashboard, InterviewPrepTool) all wrap their JSON.parse in try/catch — this one does not.
mediumLow.fix: Wrap in try/catch: `try { const s = sessionStorage.getItem('userData'); if (s && s !== 'undefined' && s !== 'null') setUserData(JSON.parse(s)); } catch (e) { console.warn('Bad userData in sessionStorage', e); }`.

mediumLow.title: Profile-analysis progress setInterval leaks if user navigates away mid-analysis
mediumLow.description: handleAnalyzeProfile starts `const interval = setInterval(() => setProfileAnalysis(prev => ({...prev, progress: Math.min(prev.progress + 15, 95)})), 500)`. It is only cleared inside the try/catch of the same async function (lines 138/144). If the user unmounts the component (navigates away) while the awaited aiCareerCoachApi.analyzeProfile() is still pending, neither clearInterval runs until the request settles, so the interval keeps calling setProfileAnalysis on an unmounted component — a React state-update-on-unmounted warning and a timer/memory leak. Because it uses the functional updater on `prev`, if profileAnalysis was reset to null elsewhere it also risks reading prev.progress of null.
mediumLow.fix: Store the interval id in a useRef and clear it in a useEffect cleanup (`return () => clearInterval(intervalRef.current)`). Guard the updater: `setProfileAnalysis(prev => prev ? {...prev, progress: Math.min((prev.progress||0)+15, 95)} : prev)`.

mediumLow.title: TensorFlow models loaded without explicit backend/readiness — silent slow-CPU or load failure on unsupported devices
mediumLow.description: nsfwjs.load(), cocoSsd.load() and toxicity.load() are called without first calling `await tf.ready()` / `tf.setBackend('webgl')`. On the toxicity model the import of @tensorflow/tfjs is present (contentModeration.js:1) but the backend is never explicitly initialized; nsfwjs/coco-ssd pull tfjs transitively. On devices where WebGL is unavailable or blocked, tfjs silently falls back to the CPU backend, making `model.classify`/`model.detect` block the main thread for seconds per image (the editor runs checkNSFW + checkDangerousObjects in parallel on every upload via Promise.all at imageModeration.js:249). Combined with the fail-open catches, a slow/failed backend also means moderation is effectively skipped. There is no tensor disposal, but classify/detect manage their own tensors so leakage is minor; the dominant risk is main-thread jank / unmoderated uploads.
mediumLow.fix: Initialize the backend once before loading models: `await tf.ready(); try { await tf.setBackend('webgl'); } catch { await tf.setBackend('cpu'); }` inside loadToxicityModel/loadNSFWModel (guarded by the existing singleton promises). Consider running heavy detection in a Web Worker, and surface a real error toast instead of failing open when model load throws (loadNSFWModel catch at imageModeration.js:38 already rethrows, but checkNSFW swallows it to {flagged:false} — log/telemetry that case).

mediumLow.title: matchScore parsing relies on parseInt coercing a regex match array
mediumLow.description: `const matchScore = parseInt(currentData.match_explanation?.match(/\d+/) || 75)`. String.prototype.match returns an array (e.g. ['82']) on success or null on failure. parseInt is then given that array; it works only because parseInt stringifies the single-element array to '82'. The `|| 75` fallback only triggers when match is null (no digits) — but if match_explanation contains a leading non-score number (e.g. 'Top 3 reasons, 82% fit') it extracts 3, not 82, silently displaying a wrong ML fit score that drives the colored score card (getScoreClass) and the headline percentage. Also parseInt has no radix.
mediumLow.fix: Be explicit: `const m = currentData.match_explanation?.match(/(\d{1,3})\s*%/) || currentData.match_explanation?.match(/\b(\d{1,3})\b/); const matchScore = m ? Math.min(100, parseInt(m[1], 10)) : 75;` — prefer a percentage pattern, take the captured group, clamp to 0–100, and pass radix 10.

mediumLow.title: Vision board PDF/collage capture clones canvas at full pixel size — large boards can OOM on mobile
mediumLow.description: handleSave clones the canvas node, forces it to currentRatio.width × currentRatio.height CSS px, appends it to document.body, and runs html2canvas at scale:1. For large aspect ratios (the ratios come from ASPECT_RATIOS and can be e.g. portrait poster sizes) plus multiple data-URL background/slot images already held in state, html2canvas allocates a backing bitmap of width*height*4 bytes plus rasterizes every data-URI image; on memory-constrained mobile browsers this can throw or silently produce a blank/black canvas, and the resulting collageBase64 PNG (toDataURL at quality 1.0) is then sent to the backend. The clone is removed only on the success path (line 1382); if html2canvas throws, the catch rejects but the appended clone is never removed (it's off-screen at z-index -9999 but stays in the DOM).
mediumLow.fix: Wrap the clone lifecycle in try/finally so the appended node is always removed even on error. Cap the html2canvas scale and/or output dimensions for very large ratios (e.g. clamp the longest side to ~2000px and let the backend upscale). Consider exporting JPEG at ~0.85 quality instead of PNG at 1.0 to cut memory and payload. Add a user-facing error toast if canvas.width/height is 0 (capture failed) instead of saving a blank collage.

mediumLow.title: Dev 404 responses trigger fallback port probing, masking real errors and firing duplicate mutations
mediumLow.description: In dev, any 404 (is404InDev) is treated as a 'connection error' and the request is silently retried against ports 5001 and 5002. A legitimate 404 (e.g. certificate not found, deleted resource) is thus re-issued up to two more times. For non-idempotent calls (POST/PUT/DELETE that happen to 404) this re-sends the mutation to other backends, and it delays/obscures genuine 404 handling that pages like VerifyCertificate rely on (err.status === 404).
mediumLow.fix: Only probe fallback ports on true network/connection failures (Failed to fetch / ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED / timeout), never on an HTTP 404. Drop is404InDev. If multi-port discovery is needed, do it once at startup with a dedicated health-check GET, not by replaying arbitrary requests.

mediumLow.title: User-supplied certificate ID injected into URL path without encoding
mediumLow.description: verifyCertificate calls apiCall(`/certificates/verify/${certId}`) with certId taken directly from the text input or QR decode, with no encodeURIComponent. IDs containing spaces, '#', '?', '/', or '%' break the request path: '#'/'?' truncate the path, '/' adds path segments, and spaces produce malformed URLs — yielding spurious failures or hitting the wrong endpoint. resumeApi.verifyResume correctly uses encodeURIComponent, so this is inconsistent.
mediumLow.fix: Encode the segment: apiCall(`/certificates/verify/${encodeURIComponent(certId)}`). Apply the same to any other place that interpolates raw user/QR input into a path.

mediumLow.title: Token renewal interval & visibility listener never cleaned up; renew failures are swallowed
mediumLow.description: A module-level setInterval(tryRenewToken, 5min) and a visibilitychange listener are registered at import time and never cleared, so they keep firing after logout (token is removed but timer still runs every 5 min) and accumulate under HMR in dev. Additionally tryRenewToken POSTs to /auth/renew-token but on a non-ok response (e.g. 401) it silently does nothing and does not trigger the logout/redirect flow, so an expired-but-present token can sit until the next real apiCall.
mediumLow.fix: Guard the interval/listener so they no-op when no token is present, and expose a cleanup (or move renewal into the auth context with proper teardown on logout). On a 401/!ok from renew-token, clear the session and route through the same 401 handling used in apiCall instead of swallowing it.

mediumLow.title: Supabase client created with no guard for missing env vars
mediumLow.description: createClient is called with import.meta.env.VITE_SUPABASE_URL / VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY unconditionally. If either env var is undefined in a given environment, createClient throws ('supabaseUrl is required') at module import, which can crash any route/bundle that imports anything transitively pulling in this client.
mediumLow.fix: Validate both vars before constructing the client and fail loudly with a clear message (or export null and have callers handle it), e.g. if (!SUPABASE_URL || !SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY) throw/log a descriptive error. Confirm both are present in every deploy's .env.

mediumLow.title: Certificate issue-date rendered through new Date() on a pre-formatted/locale string → 'Invalid Date'
mediumLow.description: The result renders new Date(verificationResult.certificate.issueDate).toLocaleDateString(). For the demo branch the issueDate is already a localized 'en-GB' string like '9 June 2026' (line 149), and backend issueDate format is unverified; passing such strings to new Date() yields 'Invalid Date' shown to the verifier, undermining trust on the public page.
mediumLow.fix: Have the backend return an ISO date and format once on display; in the meantime guard: const d = new Date(issueDate); render isNaN(d) ? String(issueDate) : d.toLocaleDateString(). Do not double-format the demo string.

mediumLow.title: No app-level error boundary / 404 route guarantee for verify pages observed
mediumLow.description: NotFound is a static page with only a 'Return Home' link and no logging, which is fine, but the verify pages have no React error boundary around them: an unexpected throw (e.g. new URL(decodedText) on a non-URL QR string in VerifyCertificate.jsx:59, which throws and is only caught because it is inside the try) or a render-time error would unmount to a blank screen on a public route. The QR branch relies on the surrounding try/catch, but any render error in the result card has no boundary.
mediumLow.fix: Wrap public/verify routes in an ErrorBoundary that renders a friendly fallback and reports the error, so a malformed QR/response cannot blank the page for an external verifier.

mediumLow.title: ECS container runs with writable root filesystem
mediumLow.description: `readonlyRootFilesystem` is set to false. Combined with the app serving `/uploads` via express.static and writing to the container FS, a writable root filesystem lets an attacker who achieves code execution drop binaries/webshells and persist. The Dockerfile correctly uses USER node, but the writable FS undermines defense in depth.
mediumLow.fix: Set readonlyRootFilesystem: true and mount a tmpfs/ephemeral volume only for the specific writable paths the app needs (e.g. /tmp and an uploads dir). Better, do not write uploads to local container disk at all - the app already uses Cloudinary; remove the express.static('/uploads') local-disk serving so user files never touch the container filesystem (they would be lost on Fargate task replacement anyway). Also add a `linuxParameters` with dropped Linux capabilities.

mediumLow.title: No ulimits, stop timeout, or appropriately sized resources; 50MB JSON body limit on 512MB task invites OOM/DoS
mediumLow.description: The task is 256 CPU / 512MB memory. The Express app accepts JSON and urlencoded bodies up to 50MB each (server.js:99-100) for base64 images. A handful of concurrent 50MB uploads, plus Mongoose maxPoolSize=50, will exhaust the 450MB Node heap and trigger the OOM killer, taking down a task - an easy unauthenticated/authenticated DoS. There is also no `memoryReservation` (soft limit), no `ulimits` (nofile), and no `stopTimeout`, so in-flight websocket connections are killed abruptly on deploy.
mediumLow.fix: Right-size to at least 512 CPU / 1024MB for a workload doing AI calls + 50MB uploads, or move large uploads off the JSON body to multipart/direct-to-Cloudinary signed uploads and drop the body limit to ~1-2MB. Add memoryReservation as a soft limit, set ulimits nofile, and set stopTimeout (e.g. 30) so websockets drain. Add request rate limiting (express-rate-limit is implied by trust proxy but not shown applied globally) and a per-route body-size cap.

mediumLow.title: CI/CD pushes :latest mutable tag and does not gate deploy on the image vulnerability scan
mediumLow.description: The workflow pushes both an immutable github.sha tag and a mutable `:latest`, and the ECS task definition references `:latest` - so re-running an old task definition or a stale service can pull an unexpected image, and rollbacks are ambiguous. `npm audit --audit-level=high` runs only against back-end deps before build and will hard-fail the pipeline on any transitive high vuln (brittle), while there is no scan of the actual built image (Trivy/ECR scan results are never checked before deploy). The frontend build runs `aws s3 sync ... --delete` and a full CloudFront `/*` invalidation on every push with a hardcoded distribution id, with no environment protection/approval on the production deploy job.
mediumLow.fix: Reference images by immutable digest/sha tag in the rendered task definition (the render step already injects the sha image - ensure the base task def does not pin :latest). Add an explicit image scan step (Trivy or `aws ecr describe-image-scan-findings`) and fail the deploy on HIGH/CRITICAL. Consider `npm audit` as non-blocking or with an allowlist to avoid pipeline brittleness, but keep a real SCA gate. Put the deploy job behind a GitHub Environment with required reviewers/branch protection, and scope the OIDC role (GithubActionsECSRole) to only the needed ECR/ECS/S3/CloudFront actions and this repo's subject claim.

mediumLow.title: ECS egress security group allows unrestricted outbound to 0.0.0.0/0 on 80 and 443
mediumLow.description: The ECS task SG permits outbound TCP 443 and TCP 80 to 0.0.0.0/0. This is broader than needed (the app only needs OpenRouter/OpenAI, Cloudinary, MongoDB Atlas, SES, Deepgram) and gives a compromised container or malicious dependency an unrestricted exfiltration/C2 channel. Port 80 outbound is justified only as 'OS updates' but a read-only, scan-on-push image should not be patching at runtime.
mediumLow.fix: Restrict egress to the specific destinations required, ideally via VPC endpoints (Secrets Manager, ECR, CloudWatch Logs, S3, SES) so that AWS-service traffic never leaves the VPC, and an egress firewall (AWS Network Firewall or a proxy with domain allowlist) for the external SaaS APIs. Remove the port-80 outbound rule. Keep MongoDB Atlas access over VPC peering/private endpoint rather than public 443.

mediumLow.title: WebSocket scaling relies on ALB cookie stickiness but raw ws auth has no stickiness/handshake protection; Redis URL built with empty creds
mediumLow.description: The plan enables ALB load-balancer-cookie stickiness for websockets. Native WebSocket (the /ws/notifications raw ws) is a single long-lived connection and does not need cookie stickiness; socket.io with the Redis adapter handles cross-pod delivery, so stickiness is mainly relevant only to socket.io's HTTP long-polling fallback. More importantly, the Redis URL is constructed as `redis://${REDIS_USERNAME||''}:${REDIS_PASSWORD||''}@host:port` - if REDIS_USERNAME/REDIS_PASSWORD are unset (and REDIS_USERNAME is NOT in the task definition secrets) it produces `redis://:@host` and, against an ElastiCache Serverless endpoint that requires TLS, uses the plaintext `redis://` scheme rather than `rediss://`, so cross-pod sync will silently fail and fall back to single-instance mode (notifications not delivered to users on other tasks). The broadcastToAll publishes userId '*' to Redis but the subscriber does `clients.get('*')` which never matches, so cross-pod broadcasts are dropped.
mediumLow.fix: Use `rediss://` (TLS) for ElastiCache transit encryption and ensure REDIS_USERNAME is provisioned (or omit the user portion entirely when using AUTH-token-only). Add REDIS_USERNAME to the task definition secrets/env. Fix broadcastToAll cross-pod path: the subscriber must handle the '*' broadcast case by iterating all local clients rather than `clients.get('*')`. Confirm socket.io path/sticky behavior end to end, and prefer forcing websocket transport (disable long-polling) to make stickiness unnecessary. Add startup verification that Redis connected, failing health if scaled mode is required.

mediumLow.title: Helmet crossOriginResourcePolicy relaxed to cross-origin and CORS allows any no-origin request including in production
mediumLow.description: helmet is configured with crossOriginResourcePolicy 'cross-origin', loosening the default same-origin resource protection. The CORS callback returns allow (callback(null,true)) for ANY request with no Origin header (`if (!origin) return callback(null, true)`) even in production - server-to-server, curl, and many automated tools omit Origin, so the 'strict' production CORS is trivially bypassed for credentialed-but-non-browser clients. The codebase comment even acknowledges the prior complaint that the 'server talks to any IP'.
mediumLow.fix: In production, do not blanket-allow missing-Origin requests for credentialed endpoints; restrict no-origin allowance to specifically intended non-browser clients via an API key/mTLS, or reject. Tighten helmet CORP back to 'same-site'/'same-origin' and serve cross-origin images via Cloudinary's CDN rather than the API. Keep the explicit FRONTEND_URL allowlist (already correct) but also handle the production case where FRONTEND_URL is undefined (currently would throw/deny silently).

mediumLow.title: WAF and TLS guidance present but no rate limiting at WAF, and HTTP listener config / TLS version inconsistency

This is a pure analysis/estimation task — no codebase investigation needed. I'll produce the cost estimate directly.

# SMAART Platform — AWS Monthly Cost Estimate (ap-south-1 Mumbai)

**FX assumption:** ~₹83 / USD. **Pricing basis:** ap-south-1 (Mumbai) on-demand list prices, mid-2025/2026 levels. AI/LLM (OpenRouter/OpenAI) and Cloudinary are **third-party SaaS — billed outside AWS** and called out separately. All figures are **realistic estimates**, not billing guarantees.

## Architecture assumptions

| Item | Assumption |
|---|---|
| Scale | Tier A: ~1,000 active users / low concurrency. Tier B: ~5,000 active users, peak ~300-500 concurrent websocket connections |
| Backend | Express/Node, persistent websockets, outbound AI/email/upload calls |
| Frontend | React static build (SPA) — served from S3 + CloudFront, **not** from ECS |
| DB | MongoDB — recommend **MongoDB Atlas on AWS Mumbai** (managed, billed via Atlas/AWS Marketplace) |
| Media | Cloudinary (SaaS, external) |
| Region | ap-south-1, single region |
| Traffic | Tier A ~150-300 GB egress/mo; Tier B ~1-2 TB egress/mo |

---

## Tier A — Budget-friendly / Startup Launch (~1,000 users)

Single-AZ-tolerant but production-hygiene compliant (managed DB, HTTPS, secrets, logs, backups).

| Service | Size / Config | USD/mo | INR/mo |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| **ECS Fargate** (backend) | 1 task, 0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, 24×7 (~1 task always-on) | ~$18 | ~₹1,500 |
| **ALB** | 1 ALB, low LCU (websockets need sticky long-lived conns) | ~$20 | ~₹1,660 |
| **MongoDB Atlas M10** | Dedicated M10, AWS Mumbai, 10 GB, daily backup | ~$60 | ~₹4,980 |
| **ECR** | ~5 GB image storage | ~$0.50 | ~₹40 |
| **CloudWatch** | Logs ~5 GB ingest + few alarms/metrics | ~$5 | ~₹415 |
| **Secrets Manager** | ~5 secrets | ~$2 | ~₹166 |
| **NAT Gateway** | 1 NAT, ~50 GB processed *(or skip — see note)* | ~$35 | ~₹2,905 |
| **S3** (frontend + uploads) | ~20 GB + requests | ~$1 | ~₹83 |
| **CloudFront** | ~200 GB egress (frontend + cached) | ~$17 | ~₹1,410 |
| **Route 53** | 1 hosted zone + queries | ~$1 | ~₹83 |
| **ACM** | TLS certs (public) | $0 | ₹0 |
| **WAF** | Optional at this tier — 1 ACL + few rules | ~$8 | ~₹664 |
| **Data transfer** | Misc inter-AZ / direct egress | ~$5 | ~₹415 |
| **Subtotal (with WAF + NAT)** | | **~$172** | **~₹14,300** |
| **Lean subtotal (no WAF, no NAT*)** | | **~$129** | **~₹10,700** |

\* **Budget NAT tip:** A single NAT Gateway (~$35/mo + data) is often the largest "hidden" line item at startup scale. If your tasks only need outbound internet (AI/email/Cloudinary) and you don't run them in private subnets for compliance reasons, you can run the Fargate task in a **public subnet with a public IP** and skip NAT entirely — saving ~$35/mo while still being production-acceptable for a single-service launch. Add NAT back the moment you have a compliance/security requirement for private subnets.

---

## Tier B — Recommended Production-Professional (HA, autoscaling, ~5,000 users)

Multi-AZ, autoscaling, WAF on, redundant NAT, larger managed DB with HA.

| Service | Size / Config | USD/mo | INR/mo |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| **ECS Fargate** (backend) | 2-6 tasks autoscaling, 1 vCPU / 2 GB; baseline ~3 tasks 24×7 | ~$130 | ~₹10,800 |
| **ALB** | 1 ALB, higher LCU (websocket concurrency, more new conns) | ~$30 | ~₹2,490 |
| **MongoDB Atlas M30** | Dedicated M30, 3-node replica set, AWS Mumbai, ~40 GB, PITR backup | ~$540 | ~₹44,800 |
| **ECR** | ~10 GB + cross-AZ pulls | ~$1.50 | ~₹125 |
| **CloudWatch** | ~30 GB logs, dashboards, alarms, Container Insights | ~$40 | ~₹3,320 |
| **Secrets Manager** | ~10 secrets + rotation | ~$5 | ~₹415 |
| **NAT Gateway** | 2 NAT (1 per AZ for HA), ~400 GB processed | ~$110 | ~₹9,130 |
| **S3** (frontend + uploads) | ~80 GB + requests + versioning | ~$3 | ~₹250 |
| **CloudFront** | ~1.5 TB egress + requests | ~$125 | ~₹10,375 |
| **Route 53** | Hosted zone + health checks + higher queries | ~$3 | ~₹250 |
| **ACM** | Public TLS certs | $0 | ₹0 |
| **WAF** | 1 ACL, managed rule groups, ~10M requests | ~$25 | ~₹2,075 |
| **Data transfer** | Inter-AZ replication, direct egress | ~$30 | ~₹2,490 |
| **Subtotal** | | **~$1,043** | **~₹86,500** |

> Add **20-30% buffer** for spikes, support plan, and metric/API overages → realistic Tier B planning number **~$1,250-1,350/mo (~₹1,03,000-1,12,000/mo)**.

---

## Fargate vs EC2 — Recommendation

**Use Fargate for both launch and early production.** Rationale:

- **No cluster management.** A launch-stage company should not pay an engineer to patch/scale EC2 container hosts. Fargate removes EC2, AMI patching, and capacity planning.
- **Websockets are fine on Fargate** behind an ALB (long-lived connections supported; just tune idle timeout and use connection draining).
- **Cost crossover:** EC2 (especially with Savings Plans / Spot) becomes cheaper only at sustained high CPU/RAM (~8-15+ vCPUs running 24×7). Below that, Fargate's premium (~20-30% per vCPU-hr) is far cheaper than the engineering time EC2 costs.
- **When to switch to EC2:** once your steady-state compute exceeds roughly **8-10 vCPUs 24×7** and you can commit to a 1-yr Savings Plan, EC2 + Cluster Auto Scaling saves meaningful money. At ~5,000 users you are **not** there yet — stay on Fargate.
- **Cost lever regardless:** buy a **1-year Fargate Compute Savings Plan** for the always-on baseline (~30% off the steady tasks) once load is predictable.

## MongoDB: Atlas vs DocumentDB vs self-managed

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **MongoDB Atlas on AWS Mumbai** | **Recommended.** True MongoDB, managed HA, backups, PITR, scaling, peering into your VPC. M10 launch → M30 prod. Billed via Atlas (USD), deploys in ap-south-1. |
| **DocumentDB** | AWS-native, but **not 100% MongoDB-compatible** (lags driver/feature versions; can break aggregation/operators). Min HA cluster (~3× t3/r6g) often costs **more** than Atlas M30 with worse compatibility. Avoid unless you want everything inside AWS billing. |
| **Self-managed on EC2** | Cheapest raw compute, but you own replica-set ops, backups, upgrades, security. **Not recommended** — false economy for a small team. |

---

## (C) What scales the cost — the real cost drivers

1. **MongoDB tier** — biggest single line item. M10→M30→M40 roughly doubles each step. Right-size by working-set RAM, not disk. Single largest lever in both tiers.
2. **CloudFront / data egress** — scales directly with media-heavy traffic and frontend bundle size. Offload media to Cloudinary (you already do) so CloudFront mostly serves the cached SPA. Egress is the #1 surprise bill at scale.
3. **Fargate task count** — autoscaling on websocket concurrency / CPU. Persistent websockets pin memory, so connections-per-task caps how low you scale. More concurrent users = more always-on tasks.
4. **NAT Gateway data processing** — every outbound AI/Cloudinary/email byte through NAT is billed (~$0.045/GB processed + hourly). Heavy AI payloads inflate this. Use a **VPC Gateway Endpoint for S3** (free) and consider interface endpoints only if they pay off.
5. **CloudWatch Logs ingestion** — verbose app/websocket logging silently balloons. Set retention (7-30 days) and sample debug logs.
6. **WAF requests** — scales with request volume; managed rule groups add per-rule + per-request cost.
7. **NOT on the AWS bill (track separately):** **OpenRouter/OpenAI** token spend (can dwarf all AWS costs — easily $200-$2,000+/mo depending on model and volume), **Cloudinary** plan (~$0-$224+/mo), and any **email** provider (SES is cheap at ~$0.10/1k; 3rd-party like SendGrid/Postmark is separate).

---

## Bottom line

| Tier | USD/mo | INR/mo |
|---|---:|---:|
| **A — Lean launch** (no WAF/NAT, Fargate, Atlas M10) | **~$130** | **~₹10,700** |
| **A — Launch w/ WAF + NAT** | **~$172** | **~₹14,300** |
| **B — Production HA** (raw) | **~$1,043** | **~₹86,500** |
| **B — Production HA** (planning w/ buffer) | **~$1,250-1,350** | **~₹1.03-1.12 L** |

**Recommended budget-friendly path that still follows production rules:** Fargate (1 task, Savings Plan when stable) + **MongoDB Atlas M10** (managed HA + backups = the production-grade part) + ALB + S3/CloudFront for the React SPA + ACM (free TLS) + Secrets Manager + scoped CloudWatch retention. Start with WAF in **count mode** and a **single NAT** (or public-subnet task to skip NAT). This lands around **$130-175/mo (~₹11,000-14,500/mo)** while keeping managed DB, HTTPS, secrets, backups, and logging — the things that actually make it "production." Remember to budget AI/LLM and Cloudinary **separately**, as those often exceed your entire AWS bill.

*Note: AWS list prices drift and Atlas/3rd-party SaaS pricing changes — validate against the AWS Pricing Calculator and live Atlas quotes before committing budget.*
